              - link "¶" [ref=e677]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "contains two field lines, both with the field name \"Example-Field\". The first field line has a field line value of \"Foo, Bar\", while the second field line value is \"Baz\". The field value for \"Example-Field\" is the list \"Foo, Bar, Baz\"."
              - link "¶" [ref=e678]
          - generic
            - heading "5.3. Field Order" [level=3, ref=e254]
              - link "5.3. " [ref=e679]
              - link "Field Order" [ref=e680]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A recipient MAY combine multiple field lines within a field section that have the same field name into one field line, without changing the semantics of the message, by appending each subsequent field line value to the initial field line value in order, separated by a comma (\",\") and optional whitespace ("
              - link "OWS" [ref=e681]
              - StaticText ", defined in "
              - link "Section 5.6.3" [ref=e682]
              - StaticText "). For consistency, use comma SP."
              - link "¶" [ref=e683]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The order in which field lines with the same name are received is therefore significant to the interpretation of the field value; a proxy MUST NOT change the order of these field line values when forwarding a message."
              - link "¶" [ref=e684]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "This means that, aside from the well-known exception noted below, a sender MUST NOT generate multiple field lines with the same name in a message (whether in the headers or trailers) or append a field line when a field line of the same name already exists in the message, unless that field's definition allows multiple field line values to be recombined as a comma-separated list (i.e., at least one alternative of the field's definition allows a comma-separated list, such as an ABNF rule of #(values) defined in "
              - link "Section 5.6.1" [ref=e685]
              - StaticText ")."
              - link "¶" [ref=e686]
            - paragraph
              - strong
                - StaticText "Note:"
              - StaticText " In practice, the \"Set-Cookie\" header field (["
              - link "COOKIE" [ref=e1752]
              - StaticText "]) often appears in a response message across multiple field lines and does not use the list syntax, violating the above requirements on multiple field lines with the same field name. Since it cannot be combined into a single field value, recipients ought to handle \"Set-Cookie\" as a special case while processing fields. (See Appendix A.2.3 of ["
              - link "Kri2001" [ref=e1753]
              - StaticText "] for details.)"
              - link "¶" [ref=e1754]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The order in which field lines with differing field names are received in a section is not significant. However, it is good practice to send header fields that contain additional control data first, such as "
              - link "Host" [ref=e687]
              - StaticText " on requests and "
              - link "Date" [ref=e688]
              - StaticText " on responses, so that implementations can decide when not to handle a message as early as possible."
              - link "¶" [ref=e689]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server MUST NOT apply a request to the target resource until it receives the entire request header section, since later header field lines might include conditionals, authentication credentials, or deliberately misleading duplicate header fields that could impact request processing."
              - link "¶" [ref=e690]
          - generic
            - heading "5.4. Field Limits" [level=3, ref=e255]
              - link "5.4. " [ref=e691]
              - link "Field Limits" [ref=e692]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "HTTP does not place a predefined limit on the length of each field line, field value, or on the length of a header or trailer section as a whole, as described in "
              - link "Section 2" [ref=e693]
              - StaticText ". Various ad hoc limitations on individual lengths are found in practice, often depending on the specific field's semantics."
              - link "¶" [ref=e694]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server that receives a request header field line, field value, or set of fields larger than it wishes to process MUST respond with an appropriate "
              - link "4xx (Client Error)" [ref=e695]
              - StaticText " status code. Ignoring such header fields would increase the server's vulnerability to request smuggling attacks ("
              - link "Section 11.2" [expanded=false, ref=e696]
              - StaticText " of ["
              - link "HTTP/1.1" [ref=e697]
              - StaticText "])."
              - link "¶" [ref=e698]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A client MAY discard or truncate received field lines that are larger than the client wishes to process if the field semantics are such that the dropped value(s) can be safely ignored without changing the message framing or response semantics."
              - link "¶" [ref=e699]
          - generic
            - heading "5.5. Field Values" [level=3, ref=e256]
              - link "5.5. " [ref=e700]
              - link "Field Values" [ref=e701]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "HTTP field values consist of a sequence of characters in a format defined by the field's grammar. Each field's grammar is usually defined using ABNF (["
              - link "RFC5234" [expanded=false, ref=e702]
              - StaticText "])."
              - link "¶" [ref=e703]
            - generic
              - generic
                - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e1755]
                - status
                - StaticText "  field-value    = *field-content\n  field-content  = field-vchar\n                   [ 1*( SP / HTAB / field-vchar ) field-vchar ]\n  field-vchar    = VCHAR / obs-text\n  obs-text       = %x80-FF\n"
              - link "¶" [ref=e704]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A field value does not include leading or trailing whitespace. When a specific version of HTTP allows such whitespace to appear in a message, a field parsing implementation MUST exclude such whitespace prior to evaluating the field value."
              - link "¶" [ref=e705]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Field values are usually constrained to the range of US-ASCII characters ["
              - link "USASCII" [ref=e706]
              - StaticText "]. Fields needing a greater range of characters can use an encoding, such as the one defined in ["
              - link "RFC8187" [expanded=false, ref=e707]
              - StaticText "]. Historically, HTTP allowed field content with text in the ISO-8859-1 charset ["
              - link "ISO-8859-1" [ref=e708]
              - StaticText "], supporting other charsets only through use of ["
              - link "RFC2047" [expanded=false, ref=e709]
              - StaticText "] encoding. Specifications for newly defined fields SHOULD limit their values to visible US-ASCII octets (VCHAR), SP, and HTAB. A recipient SHOULD treat other allowed octets in field content (i.e., "
              - link "obs-text" [ref=e710]
              - StaticText ") as opaque data."
              - link "¶" [ref=e711]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Field values containing CR, LF, or NUL characters are invalid and dangerous, due to the varying ways that implementations might parse and interpret those characters; a recipient of CR, LF, or NUL within a field value MUST either reject the message or replace each of those characters with SP before further processing or forwarding of that message. Field values containing other CTL characters are also invalid; however, recipients MAY retain such characters for the sake of robustness when they appear within a safe context (e.g., an application-specific quoted string that will not be processed by any downstream HTTP parser)."
              - link "¶" [ref=e712]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Fields that only anticipate a single member as the field value are referred to as \"singleton fields\"."
              - link "¶" [ref=e713]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Fields that allow multiple members as the field value are referred to as \"list-based fields\". The list operator extension of "
              - link "Section 5.6.1" [ref=e714]
              - StaticText " is used as a common notation for defining field values that can contain multiple members."
              - link "¶" [ref=e715]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Because commas (\",\") are used as the delimiter between members, they need to be treated with care if they are allowed as data within a member. This is true for both list-based and singleton fields, since a singleton field might be erroneously sent with multiple members and detecting such errors improves interoperability. Fields that expect to contain a comma within a member, such as within an "
              - link "HTTP-date" [ref=e716]
              - StaticText " or "
              - link "URI-reference" [ref=e717]
              - StaticText " element, ought to be defined with delimiters around that element to distinguish any comma within that data from potential list separators."
              - link "¶" [ref=e718]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "For example, a textual date and a URI (either of which might contain a comma) could be safely carried in list-based field values like these:"
              - link "¶" [ref=e719]
            - generic
              - generic
                - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e1756]
                - status
                - StaticText "Example-URIs: \"http://example.com/a.html,foo\",\n              \"http://without-a-comma.example.com/\"\nExample-Dates: \"Sat, 04 May 1996\", \"Wed, 14 Sep 2005\"\n"
              - link "¶" [ref=e720]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Note that double-quote delimiters are almost always used with the quoted-string production ("
              - link "Section 5.6.4" [ref=e721]
              - StaticText "); using a different syntax inside double-quotes will likely cause unnecessary confusion."
              - link "¶" [ref=e722]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Many fields (such as "
              - link "Content-Type" [ref=e723]
              - StaticText ", defined in "
              - link "Section 8.3" [ref=e724]
              - StaticText ") use a common syntax for parameters that allows both unquoted (token) and quoted (quoted-string) syntax for a parameter value ("
              - link "Section 5.6.6" [ref=e725]
              - StaticText "). Use of common syntax allows recipients to reuse existing parser components. When allowing both forms, the meaning of a parameter value ought to be the same whether it was received as a token or a quoted string."
              - link "¶" [ref=e726]
            - paragraph
              - strong
                - StaticText "Note:"
              - StaticText " For defining field value syntax, this specification uses an ABNF rule named after the field name to define the allowed grammar for that field's value (after said value has been extracted from the underlying messaging syntax and multiple instances combined into a list)."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1757]
          - generic
            - heading "5.6. Common Rules for Defining Field Values" [level=3, ref=e257]
              - link "5.6. " [ref=e727]
              - link "Common Rules for Defining Field Values" [ref=e728]
            - generic
              - heading "5.6.1. Lists (#rule ABNF Extension)" [level=4, ref=e1758]
                - link "5.6.1. " [ref=e2189]
                - link "Lists (#rule ABNF Extension)" [ref=e2190]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A #rule extension to the ABNF rules of ["
                - link "RFC5234" [expanded=false, ref=e2191]
                - StaticText "] is used to improve readability in the definitions of some list-based field values."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2192]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A construct \"#\" is defined, similar to \"*\", for defining comma-delimited lists of elements. The full form is \"<n>#<m>element\" indicating at least <n> and at most <m> elements, each separated by a single comma (\",\") and optional whitespace ("
                - link "OWS" [ref=e2193]
                - StaticText ", defined in "
                - link "Section 5.6.3" [ref=e2194]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2195]
              - generic
                - heading "5.6.1.1. Sender Requirements" [level=5, ref=e3741]
                  - link "5.6.1.1. " [ref=e4663]
                  - link "Sender Requirements" [ref=e4664]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "In any production that uses the list construct, a sender MUST NOT generate empty list elements. In other words, a sender has to generate lists that satisfy the following syntax:"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4665]
                - generic
                  - generic
                    - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e5013]
                    - status
                    - StaticText "  1#element => element *( OWS \",\" OWS element )\n"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4666]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "and:"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4667]
                - generic
                  - generic
                    - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e5014]
                    - status
                    - StaticText "  #element => [ 1#element ]\n"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4668]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "and for n >= 1 and m > 1:"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4669]
                - generic
                  - generic
                    - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e5015]
                    - status
                    - StaticText "  <n>#<m>element => element <n-1>*<m-1>( OWS \",\" OWS element )\n"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4670]
                - paragraph
                  - link "Appendix A" [ref=e4671]
                  - StaticText " shows the collected ABNF for senders after the list constructs have been expanded."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4672]
              - generic
                - heading "5.6.1.2. Recipient Requirements" [level=5, ref=e3742]
                  - link "5.6.1.2. " [ref=e4673]
                  - link "Recipient Requirements" [ref=e4674]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Empty elements do not contribute to the count of elements present. A recipient MUST parse and ignore a reasonable number of empty list elements: enough to handle common mistakes by senders that merge values, but not so much that they could be used as a denial-of-service mechanism. In other words, a recipient MUST accept lists that satisfy the following syntax:"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4675]
                - generic
                  - generic
                    - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e5016]
                    - status
                    - StaticText "  #element => [ element ] *( OWS \",\" OWS [ element ] )\n"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4676]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Note that because of the potential presence of empty list elements, the RFC 5234 ABNF cannot enforce the cardinality of list elements, and consequently all cases are mapped as if there was no cardinality specified."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4677]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "For example, given these ABNF productions:"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4678]
                - generic
                  - generic
                    - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e5017]
                    - status
                    - StaticText "  example-list      = 1#example-list-elmt\n  example-list-elmt = token ; see Section 5.6.2\n"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4679]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Then the following are valid values for example-list (not including the double quotes, which are present for delimitation only):"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4680]
                - generic
                  - generic
                    - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e5018]
                    - status
                    - StaticText "  \"foo,bar\"\n  \"foo ,bar,\"\n  \"foo , ,bar,charlie\"\n"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4681]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "In contrast, the following values would be invalid, since at least one non-empty element is required by the example-list production:"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4682]
                - generic
                  - generic
                    - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e5019]
                    - status
                    - StaticText "  \"\"\n  \",\"\n  \",   ,\"\n"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4683]
            - generic
              - heading "5.6.2. Tokens" [level=4, ref=e1759]
                - link "5.6.2. " [ref=e2196]
                - link "Tokens" [ref=e2197]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Tokens are short textual identifiers that do not include whitespace or delimiters."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3743]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3744]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  token          = 1*tchar\n\n  tchar          = \"!\" / \"#\" / \"$\" / \"%\" / \"&\" / \"'\" / \"*\"\n                 / \"+\" / \"-\" / \".\" / \"^\" / \"_\" / \"`\" / \"|\" / \"~\"\n                 / DIGIT / ALPHA\n                 ; any VCHAR, except delimiters\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2198]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Many HTTP field values are defined using common syntax components, separated by whitespace or specific delimiting characters. Delimiters are chosen from the set of US-ASCII visual characters not allowed in a "
                - link "token" [ref=e3745]
                - StaticText " (DQUOTE and \"(),/:;<=>?@[\\]{}\")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3746]
            - generic
              - heading "5.6.3. Whitespace" [level=4, ref=e1760]
                - link "5.6.3. " [ref=e2199]
                - link "Whitespace" [ref=e2200]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "This specification uses three rules to denote the use of linear whitespace: OWS (optional whitespace), RWS (required whitespace), and BWS (\"bad\" whitespace)."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2201]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The OWS rule is used where zero or more linear whitespace octets might appear. For protocol elements where optional whitespace is preferred to improve readability, a sender SHOULD generate the optional whitespace as a single SP; otherwise, a sender SHOULD NOT generate optional whitespace except as needed to overwrite invalid or unwanted protocol elements during in-place message filtering."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2202]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The RWS rule is used when at least one linear whitespace octet is required to separate field tokens. A sender SHOULD generate RWS as a single SP."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2203]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "OWS and RWS have the same semantics as a single SP. Any content known to be defined as OWS or RWS MAY be replaced with a single SP before interpreting it or forwarding the message downstream."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2204]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The BWS rule is used where the grammar allows optional whitespace only for historical reasons. A sender MUST NOT generate BWS in messages. A recipient MUST parse for such bad whitespace and remove it before interpreting the protocol element."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2205]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "BWS has no semantics. Any content known to be defined as BWS MAY be removed before interpreting it or forwarding the message downstream."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2206]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3747]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  OWS            = *( SP / HTAB )\n                 ; optional whitespace\n  RWS            = 1*( SP / HTAB )\n                 ; required whitespace\n  BWS            = OWS\n                 ; \"bad\" whitespace\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2207]
            - generic
              - heading "5.6.4. Quoted Strings" [level=4, ref=e1761]
                - link "5.6.4. " [ref=e2208]
                - link "Quoted Strings" [ref=e2209]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A string of text is parsed as a single value if it is quoted using double-quote marks."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3748]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3749]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  quoted-string  = DQUOTE *( qdtext / quoted-pair ) DQUOTE\n  qdtext         = HTAB / SP / %x21 / %x23-5B / %x5D-7E / obs-text\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2210]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The backslash octet (\"\\\") can be used as a single-octet quoting mechanism within quoted-string and comment constructs. Recipients that process the value of a quoted-string MUST handle a quoted-pair as if it were replaced by the octet following the backslash."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3750]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3751]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  quoted-pair    = \"\\\" ( HTAB / SP / VCHAR / obs-text )\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2211]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A sender SHOULD NOT generate a quoted-pair in a quoted-string except where necessary to quote DQUOTE and backslash octets occurring within that string. A sender SHOULD NOT generate a quoted-pair in a comment except where necessary to quote parentheses [\"(\" and \")\"] and backslash octets occurring within that comment."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2212]
            - generic
              - heading "5.6.5. Comments" [level=4, ref=e1762]
                - link "5.6.5. " [ref=e2213]
                - link "Comments" [ref=e2214]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Comments can be included in some HTTP fields by surrounding the comment text with parentheses. Comments are only allowed in fields containing \"comment\" as part of their field value definition."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3752]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3753]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  comment        = \"(\" *( ctext / quoted-pair / comment ) \")\"\n  ctext          = HTAB / SP / %x21-27 / %x2A-5B / %x5D-7E / obs-text\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2215]
            - generic
              - heading "5.6.6. Parameters" [level=4, ref=e1763]
                - link "5.6.6. " [ref=e2216]
                - link "Parameters" [ref=e2217]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Parameters are instances of name/value pairs; they are often used in field values as a common syntax for appending auxiliary information to an item. Each parameter is usually delimited by an immediately preceding semicolon."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3754]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3755]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  parameters      = *( OWS \";\" OWS [ parameter ] )\n  parameter       = parameter-name \"=\" parameter-value\n  parameter-name  = token\n  parameter-value = ( token / quoted-string )\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2218]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Parameter names are case-insensitive. Parameter values might or might not be case-sensitive, depending on the semantics of the parameter name. Examples of parameters and some equivalent forms can be seen in media types ("
                - link "Section 8.3.1" [ref=e2219]
                - StaticText ") and the Accept header field ("
                - link "Section 12.5.1" [ref=e2220]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2221]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A parameter value that matches the "
                - link "token" [ref=e2222]
                - StaticText " production can be transmitted either as a token or within a quoted-string. The quoted and unquoted values are equivalent."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2223]
              - paragraph
                - strong
                  - StaticText "Note:"
                - StaticText " Parameters do not allow whitespace (not even \"bad\" whitespace) around the \"=\" character."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3756]
            - generic
              - heading "5.6.7. Date/Time Formats" [level=4, ref=e1764]
                - link "5.6.7. " [ref=e2224]
                - link "Date/Time Formats" [ref=e2225]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Prior to 1995, there were three different formats commonly used by servers to communicate timestamps. For compatibility with old implementations, all three are defined here. The preferred format is a fixed-length and single-zone subset of the date and time specification used by the Internet Message Format ["
                - link "RFC5322" [expanded=false, ref=e2226]
                - StaticText "]."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2227]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3757]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  HTTP-date    = IMF-fixdate / obs-date\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2228]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An example of the preferred format is"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2229]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3758]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT    ; IMF-fixdate\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2230]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Examples of the two obsolete formats are"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2231]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3759]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Sunday, 06-Nov-94 08:49:37 GMT   ; obsolete RFC 850 format\n  Sun Nov  6 08:49:37 1994         ; ANSI C's asctime() format\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2232]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A recipient that parses a timestamp value in an HTTP field MUST accept all three HTTP-date formats. When a sender generates a field that contains one or more timestamps defined as HTTP-date, the sender MUST generate those timestamps in the IMF-fixdate format."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2233]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An HTTP-date value represents time as an instance of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). The first two formats indicate UTC by the three-letter abbreviation for Greenwich Mean Time, \"GMT\", a predecessor of the UTC name; values in the asctime format are assumed to be in UTC."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2234]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A \"clock\" is an implementation capable of providing a reasonable approximation of the current instant in UTC. A clock implementation ought to use NTP (["
                - link "RFC5905" [expanded=false, ref=e2235]
                - StaticText "]), or some similar protocol, to synchronize with UTC."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2236]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Preferred format:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3760]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3761]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  IMF-fixdate  = day-name \",\" SP date1 SP time-of-day SP GMT\n  ; fixed length/zone/capitalization subset of the format\n  ; see Section 3.3 of [RFC5322]\n\n  day-name     = %s\"Mon\" / %s\"Tue\" / %s\"Wed\"\n               / %s\"Thu\" / %s\"Fri\" / %s\"Sat\" / %s\"Sun\"\n\n  date1        = day SP month SP year\n               ; e.g., 02 Jun 1982\n\n  day          = 2DIGIT\n  month        = %s\"Jan\" / %s\"Feb\" / %s\"Mar\" / %s\"Apr\"\n               / %s\"May\" / %s\"Jun\" / %s\"Jul\" / %s\"Aug\"\n               / %s\"Sep\" / %s\"Oct\" / %s\"Nov\" / %s\"Dec\"\n  year         = 4DIGIT\n\n  GMT          = %s\"GMT\"\n\n  time-of-day  = hour \":\" minute \":\" second\n               ; 00:00:00 - 23:59:60 (leap second)\n\n  hour         = 2DIGIT\n  minute       = 2DIGIT\n  second       = 2DIGIT\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2237]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Obsolete formats:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3762]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3763]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  obs-date     = rfc850-date / asctime-date\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2238]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3764]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  rfc850-date  = day-name-l \",\" SP date2 SP time-of-day SP GMT\n  date2        = day \"-\" month \"-\" 2DIGIT\n               ; e.g., 02-Jun-82\n\n  day-name-l   = %s\"Monday\" / %s\"Tuesday\" / %s\"Wednesday\"\n               / %s\"Thursday\" / %s\"Friday\" / %s\"Saturday\"\n               / %s\"Sunday\"\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2239]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3765]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  asctime-date = day-name SP date3 SP time-of-day SP year\n  date3        = month SP ( 2DIGIT / ( SP 1DIGIT ))\n               ; e.g., Jun  2\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2240]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "HTTP-date is case sensitive. Note that "
                - link "Section 4.2" [expanded=false, ref=e2241]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "CACHING" [ref=e2242]
                - StaticText "] relaxes this for cache recipients."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2243]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A sender MUST NOT generate additional whitespace in an HTTP-date beyond that specifically included as SP in the grammar. The semantics of "
                - link "day-name" [ref=e2244]
                - StaticText ", "
                - link "day" [ref=e2245]
                - StaticText ", "
                - link "month" [ref=e2246]
                - StaticText ", "
                - link "year" [ref=e2247]
                - StaticText ", and "
                - link "time-of-day" [ref=e2248]
                - StaticText " are the same as those defined for the Internet Message Format constructs with the corresponding name (["
                - link "RFC5322" [expanded=false, ref=e2249]
                - StaticText "], "
                - link "Section 3.3" [expanded=false, ref=e2250]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2251]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Recipients of a timestamp value in rfc850-date format, which uses a two-digit year, MUST interpret a timestamp that appears to be more than 50 years in the future as representing the most recent year in the past that had the same last two digits."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2252]

        - generic
          - heading "6. Message Abstraction" [level=2, ref=e32]
            - link "6. " [ref=e94]
            - link "Message Abstraction" [ref=e95]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Each major version of HTTP defines its own syntax for communicating messages. This section defines an abstract data type for HTTP messages based on a generalization of those message characteristics, common structure, and capacity for conveying semantics. This abstraction is used to define requirements on senders and recipients that are independent of the HTTP version, such that a message in one version can be relayed through other versions without changing its meaning."
            - link "¶" [ref=e96]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "A \"message\" consists of the following:"
            - link "¶" [ref=e97]
          - list
            - listitem [level=1]
              - ListMarker "• "
              - StaticText "control data to describe and route the message,"
              - link "¶" [ref=e258]
            - listitem [level=1]
              - ListMarker "• "
              - StaticText "a headers lookup table of name/value pairs for extending that control data and conveying additional information about the sender, message, content, or context,"
              - link "¶" [ref=e259]
            - listitem [level=1]
              - ListMarker "• "
              - StaticText "a potentially unbounded stream of content, and"
              - link "¶" [ref=e260]
            - listitem [level=1]
              - ListMarker "• "
              - StaticText "a trailers lookup table of name/value pairs for communicating information obtained while sending the content."
              - link "¶" [ref=e261]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Framing and control data is sent first, followed by a header section containing fields for the headers table. When a message includes content, the content is sent after the header section, potentially followed by a trailer section that might contain fields for the trailers table."
            - link "¶" [ref=e98]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Messages are expected to be processed as a stream, wherein the purpose of that stream and its continued processing is revealed while being read. Hence, control data describes what the recipient needs to know immediately, header fields describe what needs to be known before receiving content, the content (when present) presumably contains what the recipient wants or needs to fulfill the message semantics, and trailer fields provide optional metadata that was unknown prior to sending the content."
            - link "¶" [ref=e99]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Messages are intended to be \"self-descriptive\": everything a recipient needs to know about the message can be determined by looking at the message itself, after decoding or reconstituting parts that have been compressed or elided in transit, without requiring an understanding of the sender's current application state (established via prior messages). However, a client MUST retain knowledge of the request when parsing, interpreting, or caching a corresponding response. For example, responses to the "
            - link "HEAD" [ref=e100]
            - StaticText " method look just like the beginning of a response to "
            - link "GET" [ref=e101]
            - StaticText " but cannot be parsed in the same manner."
            - link "¶" [ref=e102]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Note that this message abstraction is a generalization across many versions of HTTP, including features that might not be found in some versions. For example, trailers were introduced within the HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer coding as a trailer section after the content. An equivalent feature is present in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 within the header block that terminates each stream."
            - link "¶" [ref=e103]
          - generic
            - heading "6.1. Framing and Completeness" [level=3, ref=e262]
              - link "6.1. " [ref=e729]
              - link "Framing and Completeness" [ref=e730]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Message framing indicates how each message begins and ends, such that each message can be distinguished from other messages or noise on the same connection. Each major version of HTTP defines its own framing mechanism."
              - link "¶" [ref=e731]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "HTTP/0.9 and early deployments of HTTP/1.0 used closure of the underlying connection to end a response. For backwards compatibility, this implicit framing is also allowed in HTTP/1.1. However, implicit framing can fail to distinguish an incomplete response if the connection closes early. For that reason, almost all modern implementations use explicit framing in the form of length-delimited sequences of message data."
              - link "¶" [ref=e732]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A message is considered \"complete\" when all of the octets indicated by its framing are available. Note that, when no explicit framing is used, a response message that is ended by the underlying connection's close is considered complete even though it might be indistinguishable from an incomplete response, unless a transport-level error indicates that it is not complete."
              - link "¶" [ref=e733]
          - generic
            - heading "6.2. Control Data" [level=3, ref=e263]
              - link "6.2. " [ref=e734]
              - link "Control Data" [ref=e735]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Messages start with control data that describe its primary purpose. Request message control data includes a request method ("
              - link "Section 9" [ref=e736]
              - StaticText "), request target ("
              - link "Section 7.1" [ref=e737]
              - StaticText "), and protocol version ("
              - link "Section 2.5" [ref=e738]
              - StaticText "). Response message control data includes a status code ("
              - link "Section 15" [ref=e739]
              - StaticText "), optional reason phrase, and protocol version."
              - link "¶" [ref=e740]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "In HTTP/1.1 (["
              - link "HTTP/1.1" [ref=e741]
              - StaticText "]) and earlier, control data is sent as the first line of a message. In HTTP/2 (["
              - link "HTTP/2" [ref=e742]
              - StaticText "]) and HTTP/3 (["
              - link "HTTP/3" [ref=e743]
              - StaticText "]), control data is sent as pseudo-header fields with a reserved name prefix (e.g., \":authority\")."
              - link "¶" [ref=e744]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Every HTTP message has a protocol version. Depending on the version in use, it might be identified within the message explicitly or inferred by the connection over which the message is received. Recipients use that version information to determine limitations or potential for later communication with that sender."
              - link "¶" [ref=e745]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "When a message is forwarded by an intermediary, the protocol version is updated to reflect the version used by that intermediary. The "
              - link "Via" [ref=e746]
              - StaticText " header field ("
              - link "Section 7.6.3" [ref=e747]
              - StaticText ") is used to communicate upstream protocol information within a forwarded message."
              - link "¶" [ref=e748]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A client SHOULD send a request version equal to the highest version to which the client is conformant and whose major version is no higher than the highest version supported by the server, if this is known. A client MUST NOT send a version to which it is not conformant."
              - link "¶" [ref=e749]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A client MAY send a lower request version if it is known that the server incorrectly implements the HTTP specification, but only after the client has attempted at least one normal request and determined from the response status code or header fields (e.g., "
              - link "Server" [ref=e750]
              - StaticText ") that the server improperly handles higher request versions."
              - link "¶" [ref=e751]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server SHOULD send a response version equal to the highest version to which the server is conformant that has a major version less than or equal to the one received in the request. A server MUST NOT send a version to which it is not conformant. A server can send a "
              - link "505 (HTTP Version Not Supported)" [ref=e752]
              - StaticText " response if it wishes, for any reason, to refuse service of the client's major protocol version."
              - link "¶" [ref=e753]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A recipient that receives a message with a major version number that it implements and a minor version number higher than what it implements SHOULD process the message as if it were in the highest minor version within that major version to which the recipient is conformant. A recipient can assume that a message with a higher minor version, when sent to a recipient that has not yet indicated support for that higher version, is sufficiently backwards-compatible to be safely processed by any implementation of the same major version."
              - link "¶" [ref=e754]

              - link "Section 6.5" [ref=e765]

            - heading "6.5. Trailer Fields" [level=3, ref=e266]
              - link "6.5. " [ref=e767]
              - link "Trailer Fields" [ref=e768]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Fields ("
              - link "Section 5" [ref=e769]
              - StaticText ") that are located within a \"trailer section\" are referred to as \"trailer fields\" (or just \"trailers\", colloquially). Trailer fields can be useful for supplying message integrity checks, digital signatures, delivery metrics, or post-processing status information."
              - link "¶" [ref=e770]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Trailer fields ought to be processed and stored separately from the fields in the header section to avoid contradicting message semantics known at the time the header section was complete. The presence or absence of certain header fields might impact choices made for the routing or processing of the message as a whole before the trailers are received; those choices cannot be unmade by the later discovery of trailer fields."
              - link "¶" [ref=e771]
            - generic
              - heading "6.5.1. Limitations on Use of Trailers" [level=4, ref=e1770]
                - link "6.5.1. " [ref=e2288]
                - link "Limitations on Use of Trailers" [ref=e2289]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A trailer section is only possible when supported by the version of HTTP in use and enabled by an explicit framing mechanism. For example, the chunked transfer coding in HTTP/1.1 allows a trailer section to be sent after the content ("
                - link "Section 7.1.2" [expanded=false, ref=e2290]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "HTTP/1.1" [ref=e2291]
                - StaticText "])."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2292]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Many fields cannot be processed outside the header section because their evaluation is necessary prior to receiving the content, such as those that describe message framing, routing, authentication, request modifiers, response controls, or content format. A sender MUST NOT generate a trailer field unless the sender knows the corresponding header field name's definition permits the field to be sent in trailers."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2293]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Trailer fields can be difficult to process by intermediaries that forward messages from one protocol version to another. If the entire message can be buffered in transit, some intermediaries could merge trailer fields into the header section (as appropriate) before it is forwarded. However, in most cases, the trailers are simply discarded. A recipient MUST NOT merge a trailer field into a header section unless the recipient understands the corresponding header field definition and that definition explicitly permits and defines how trailer field values can be safely merged."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2294]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The presence of the keyword \"trailers\" in the TE header field ("
                - link "Section 10.1.4" [ref=e2295]
                - StaticText ") of a request indicates that the client is willing to accept trailer fields, on behalf of itself and any downstream clients. For requests from an intermediary, this implies that all downstream clients are willing to accept trailer fields in the forwarded response. Note that the presence of \"trailers\" does not mean that the client(s) will process any particular trailer field in the response; only that the trailer section(s) will not be dropped by any of the clients."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2296]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Because of the potential for trailer fields to be discarded in transit, a server SHOULD NOT generate trailer fields that it believes are necessary for the user agent to receive."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2297]
            - generic
              - heading "6.5.2. Processing Trailer Fields" [level=4, ref=e1771]
                - link "6.5.2. " [ref=e2298]
                - link "Processing Trailer Fields" [ref=e2299]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Trailer\" header field ("
                - link "Section 6.6.2" [ref=e2300]
                - StaticText ") can be sent to indicate fields likely to be sent in the trailer section, which allows recipients to prepare for their receipt before processing the content. For example, this could be useful if a field name indicates that a dynamic checksum should be calculated as the content is received and then immediately checked upon receipt of the trailer field value."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2301]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Like header fields, trailer fields with the same name are processed in the order received; multiple trailer field lines with the same name have the equivalent semantics as appending the multiple values as a list of members. Trailer fields that might be generated more than once during a message MUST be defined as a list-based field even if each member value is only processed once per field line received."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2302]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "At the end of a message, a recipient MAY treat the set of received trailer fields as a data structure of name/value pairs, similar to (but separate from) the header fields. Additional processing expectations, if any, can be defined within the field specification for a field intended for use in trailers."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2303]
          - generic
            - heading "6.6. Message Metadata" [level=3, ref=e267]
              - link "6.6. " [ref=e772]
              - link "Message Metadata" [ref=e773]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Fields that describe the message itself, such as when and how the message has been generated, can appear in both requests and responses."
              - link "¶" [ref=e774]
            - generic
              - heading "6.6.1. Date" [level=4, ref=e1772]
                - link "6.6.1. " [ref=e2304]
                - link "Date" [ref=e2305]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Date\" header field represents the date and time at which the message was originated, having the same semantics as the Origination Date Field (orig-date) defined in "
                - link "Section 3.6.1" [expanded=false, ref=e2306]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "RFC5322" [expanded=false, ref=e2307]
                - StaticText "]. The field value is an HTTP-date, as defined in "
                - link "Section 5.6.7" [ref=e2308]
                - StaticText "."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2309]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3787]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Date = HTTP-date\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2310]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An example is"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2311]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3788]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "Date: Tue, 15 Nov 1994 08:12:31 GMT\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2312]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A sender that generates a Date header field SHOULD generate its field value as the best available approximation of the date and time of message generation. In theory, the date ought to represent the moment just before generating the message content. In practice, a sender can generate the date value at any time during message origination."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2313]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An origin server with a clock (as defined in "
                - link "Section 5.6.7" [ref=e2314]
                - StaticText ") MUST generate a Date header field in all "
                - link "2xx (Successful)" [ref=e2315]
                - StaticText ", "
                - link "3xx (Redirection)" [ref=e2316]
                - StaticText ", and "
                - link "4xx (Client Error)" [ref=e2317]
                - StaticText " responses, and MAY generate a Date header field in "
                - link "1xx (Informational)" [ref=e2318]
                - StaticText " and "
                - link "5xx (Server Error)" [ref=e2319]
                - StaticText " responses."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2320]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An origin server without a clock MUST NOT generate a Date header field."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2321]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A recipient with a clock that receives a response message without a Date header field MUST record the time it was received and append a corresponding Date header field to the message's header section if it is cached or forwarded downstream."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2322]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A recipient with a clock that receives a response with an invalid Date header field value MAY replace that value with the time that response was received."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2323]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A user agent MAY send a Date header field in a request, though generally will not do so unless it is believed to convey useful information to the server.                 - link "¶" [ref=e2324]

            - heading "7.6. Message Forwarding" [level=3, ref=e273]
              - link "7.6. " [ref=e826]
              - link "Message Forwarding" [ref=e827]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "As described in "
              - link "Section 3.7" [ref=e828]
              - StaticText ", intermediaries can serve a variety of roles in the processing of HTTP requests and responses. Some intermediaries are used to improve performance or availability. Others are used for access control or to filter content. Since an HTTP stream has characteristics similar to a pipe-and-filter architecture, there are no inherent limits to the extent an intermediary can enhance (or interfere) with either direction of the stream."
              - link "¶" [ref=e829]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Intermediaries are expected to forward messages even when protocol elements are not recognized (e.g., new methods, status codes, or field names) since that preserves extensibility for downstream recipients."
              - link "¶" [ref=e830]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "An intermediary not acting as a tunnel MUST implement the "
              - link "Connection" [ref=e831]
              - StaticText " header field, as specified in "
              - link "Section 7.6.1" [ref=e832]
              - StaticText ", and exclude fields from being forwarded that are only intended for the incoming connection."
              - link "¶" [ref=e833]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "An intermediary MUST NOT forward a message to itself unless it is protected from an infinite request loop. In general, an intermediary ought to recognize its own server names, including any aliases, local variations, or literal IP addresses, and respond to such requests directly."
              - link "¶" [ref=e834]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "An HTTP message can be parsed as a stream for incremental processing or forwarding downstream. However, senders and recipients cannot rely on incremental delivery of partial messages, since some implementations will buffer or delay message forwarding for the sake of network efficiency, security checks, or content transformations."
              - link "¶" [ref=e835]

                - StaticText "The Max-Forwards value is a decimal integer indicating the remaining number of times this request message can be forwarded."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2371]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Each intermediary that receives a TRACE or OPTIONS request containing a Max-Forwards header field MUST check and update its value prior to forwarding the request. If the received Max-Forwards value is greater than zero, the intermediary MUST generate an updated Max-Forwards field in the forwarded message with a field value that is the lesser of a) the received value decremented by one (1) or b) the recipient's maximum supported value for Max-Forwards."

              - heading "7.6.3. Via" [level=4, ref=e1785]
                - link "7.6.3. " [ref=e2374]
                - link "Via" [ref=e2375]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Via\" header field indicates the presence of intermediate protocols and recipients between the user agent and the server (on requests) or between the origin server and the client (on responses), similar to the \"Received\" header field in email ("
                - link "Section 3.6.7" [expanded=false, ref=e2376]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "RFC5322" [expanded=false, ref=e2377]
                - StaticText "]). Via can be used for tracking message forwards, avoiding request loops, and identifying the protocol capabilities of senders along the request/response chain."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2378]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3805]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Via = #( received-protocol RWS received-by [ RWS comment ] )\n\n  received-protocol = [ protocol-name \"/\" ] protocol-version\n                    ; see Section 7.8\n  received-by       = pseudonym [ \":\" port ]\n  pseudonym         = token\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2379]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Each member of the Via field value represents a proxy or gateway that has forwarded the message. Each intermediary appends its own information about how the message was received, such that the end result is ordered according to the sequence of forwarding recipients."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2380]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A proxy MUST send an appropriate Via header field, as described below, in each message that it forwards. An HTTP-to-HTTP gateway MUST send an appropriate Via header field in each inbound request message and MAY send a Via header field in forwarded response messages."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2381]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For each intermediary, the received-protocol indicates the protocol and protocol version used by the upstream sender of the message. Hence, the Via field value records the advertised protocol capabilities of the request/response chain such that they remain visible to downstream recipients; this can be useful for determining what backwards-incompatible features might be safe to use in response, or within a later request, as described in "
                - link "Section 2.5" [ref=e2382]
                - StaticText ". For brevity, the protocol-name is omitted when the received protocol is HTTP."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2383]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The received-by portion is normally the host and optional port number of a recipient server or client that subsequently forwarded the message. However, if the real host is considered to be sensitive information, a sender MAY replace it with a pseudonym. If a port is not provided, a recipient MAY interpret that as meaning it was received on the default port, if any, for the received-protocol."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2384]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A sender MAY generate comments to identify the software of each recipient, analogous to the "
                - link "User-Agent" [ref=e2385]
                - StaticText " and "
                - link "Server" [ref=e2386]
                - StaticText " header fields. However, comments in Via are optional, and a recipient MAY remove them prior to forwarding the message."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2387]

The request received by www.example.com would then have the following Via header field:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2388]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3806]
                  - status

                - link "¶" [ref=e2389]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An intermediary used as a portal through a network firewall SHOULD NOT forward the names and ports of hosts within the firewall region unless it is explicitly enabled to do so. If not enabled, such an intermediary SHOULD replace each received-by host of any host behind the firewall by an appropriate pseudonym for that host."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2390]
              - paragraph

              - paragraph

                - link "¶" [ref=e2395]
          - generic
            - heading "7.7. Message Transformations" [level=3, ref=e274]
              - link "7.7. " [ref=e836]
              - link "Message Transformations" [ref=e837]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Some intermediaries include features for transforming messages and their content. A proxy might, for example, convert between image formats in order to save cache space or to reduce the amount of traffic on a slow link. However, operational problems might occur when these transformations are applied to content intended for critical applications, such as medical imaging or scientific data analysis, particularly when integrity checks or digital signatures are used to ensure that the content received is identical to the original."
              - link "¶" [ref=e838]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "An HTTP-to-HTTP proxy is called a \"transforming proxy\" if it is designed or configured to modify messages in a semantically meaningful way (i.e., modifications, beyond those required by normal HTTP processing, that change the message in a way that would be significant to the original sender or potentially significant to downstream recipients). For example, a transforming proxy might be acting as a shared annotation server (modifying responses to include references to a local annotation database), a malware filter, a format transcoder, or a privacy filter. Such transformations are presumed to be desired by whichever client (or client organization) chose the proxy."
              - link "¶" [ref=e839]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "If a proxy receives a target URI with a host name that is not a fully qualified domain name, it MAY add its own domain to the host name it received when forwarding the request. A proxy MUST NOT change the host name if the target URI contains a fully qualified domain name."
              - link "¶" [ref=e840]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A proxy MUST NOT modify the \"absolute-path\" and \"query\" parts of the received target URI when forwarding it to the next inbound server except as required by that forwarding protocol.               - link "Section 3.2.1" [expanded=false, ref=e841]

              - link "Section 3.2.4" [expanded=false, ref=e843]
              - StaticText " of ["
              - link "HTTP/1.1" [ref=e844]
              - StaticText "]), depending on the request method."
              - link "¶" [ref=e845]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A proxy MUST NOT transform the content ("
              - link "Section 6.4" [ref=e846]

              - link "Section 5.2.2.6" [expanded=false, ref=e847]

              - StaticText "])."

            - heading "7.8. Upgrade" [level=3, ref=e275]
              - link "7.8. " [ref=e858]
              - link "Upgrade" [ref=e859]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The \"Upgrade\" header field is intended to provide a simple mechanism for transitioning from HTTP/1.1 to some other protocol on the same connection."
              - link "¶" [ref=e860]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A client MAY send a list of protocol names in the Upgrade header field of a request to invite the server to switch to one or more of the named protocols, in order of descending preference, before sending the final response. A server MAY ignore a received Upgrade header field if it wishes to continue using the current protocol on that connection. Upgrade cannot be used to insist on a protocol change."
              - link "¶" [ref=e861]
            - generic
              - generic
                - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e1786]
                - status
                - StaticText "  Upgrade          = #protocol\n\n  protocol         = protocol-name [\"/\" protocol-version]\n  protocol-name    = token\n  protocol-version = token\n"
              - link "¶" [ref=e862]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Although protocol names are registered with a preferred case, recipients SHOULD use case-insensitive comparison when matching each protocol-name to supported protocols."
              - link "¶" [ref=e863]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server that sends a "
              - link "101 (Switching Protocols)" [ref=e864]
              - StaticText " response MUST send an Upgrade header field to indicate the new protocol(s) to which the connection is being switched; if multiple protocol layers are being switched, the sender MUST list the protocols in layer-ascending order. A server MUST NOT switch to a protocol that was not indicated by the client in the corresponding request's Upgrade header field. A server MAY choose to ignore the order of preference indicated by the client and select the new protocol(s) based on other factors, such as the nature of the request or the current load on the server."
              - link "¶" [ref=e865]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server that sends a "
              - link "426 (Upgrade Required)" [ref=e866]
              - StaticText " response MUST send an Upgrade header field to indicate the acceptable protocols, in order of descending preference."
              - link "¶" [ref=e867]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server MAY send an Upgrade header field in any other response to advertise that it implements support for upgrading to the listed protocols, in order of descending preference, when appropriate for a future request."
              - link "¶" [ref=e868]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The following is a hypothetical example sent by a client:"
              - link "¶" [ref=e869]
            - generic
              - generic
                - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e1787]
                - status
                - StaticText "GET /hello HTTP/1.1\nHost: www.example.com\nConnection: upgrade\nUpgrade: websocket, IRC/6.9, RTA/x11\n\n"
              - link "¶" [ref=e870]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The capabilities and nature of the application-level communication after the protocol change is entirely dependent upon the new protocol(s) chosen. However, immediately after sending the "
              - link "101 (Switching Protocols)" [ref=e871]
              - StaticText " response, the server is expected to continue responding to the original request as if it had received its equivalent within the new protocol (i.e., the server still has an outstanding request to satisfy after the protocol has been changed, and is expected to do so without requiring the request to be repeated)."
              - link "¶" [ref=e872]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "For example, if the Upgrade header field is received in a GET request and the server decides to switch protocols, it first responds with a "
              - link "101 (Switching Protocols)" [ref=e873]
              - StaticText " message in HTTP/1.1 and then immediately follows that with the new protocol's equivalent of a response to a GET on the target resource. This allows a connection to be upgraded to protocols with the same semantics as HTTP without the latency cost of an additional round trip. A server MUST NOT switch protocols unless the received message semantics can be honored by the new protocol; an OPTIONS request can be honored by any protocol."
              - link "¶" [ref=e874]

              - link "Expect" [ref=e880]

              - link "3xx (Redirection)" [ref=e885]

              - link "RFC2046" [expanded=false, ref=e910]

              - link "¶" [ref=e912]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "In practice, resource owners do not always properly configure their origin server to provide the correct Content-Type for a given representation. Some user agents examine the content and, in certain cases, override the received type (for example, see ["
              - link "Sniffing" [ref=e913]
              - StaticText "]). This \"MIME sniffing\" risks drawing incorrect conclusions about the data, which might expose the user to additional security risks (e.g., \"privilege escalation\").             - paragraph

              - link "Content-Type" [ref=e918]
              - StaticText " header field. Content-Encoding is primarily used to allow a representation's data to be compressed without losing the identity of its underlying media type."

                - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e1795]

              - StaticText "If one or more encodings have been applied to a representation, the sender that applied the encodings MUST generate a Content-Encoding header field that lists the content codings in the order in which they were applied.               - link "Accept-Encoding" [ref=e923]
                - StaticText "Accept-Encoding"
              - StaticText " and thus SHOULD NOT be included."
              - link "¶" [ref=e924]

              - StaticText "]), the codings listed in Content-Encoding are a characteristic of the representation; the representation is defined in terms of the coded form, and all other metadata about the representation is about the coded form unless otherwise noted in the metadata definition.               - link "¶" [ref=e928]

              - link "Content-Type" [ref=e929]
              - StaticText " or Content-Encoding, since some user agents will behave differently in their handling of each response (e.g., open a \"Save as ...\" dialog instead of automatic decompression and rendering of content)."
