              - heading "9.3.6. CONNECT" [level=4, ref=e1825]
                - link "9.3.6. " [ref=e2631]
                - link "CONNECT" [ref=e2632]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The CONNECT method requests that the recipient establish a tunnel to the destination origin server identified by the request target and, if successful, thereafter restrict its behavior to blind forwarding of data, in both directions, until the tunnel is closed. Tunnels are commonly used to create an end-to-end virtual connection, through one or more proxies, which can then be secured using TLS (Transport Layer Security, ["
                - link "TLS13" [ref=e2633]
                - StaticText "])."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2634]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "CONNECT uses a special form of request target, unique to this method, consisting of only the host and port number of the tunnel destination, separated by a colon. There is no default port; a client MUST send the port number even if the CONNECT request is based on a URI reference that contains an authority component with an elided port ("
                - link "Section 4.1" [ref=e2635]
                - StaticText "). For example,"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2636]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3873]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "CONNECT server.example.com:80 HTTP/1.1\nHost: server.example.com\n\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2637]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A server MUST reject a CONNECT request that targets an empty or invalid port number, typically by responding with a 400 (Bad Request) status code."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2638]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Because CONNECT changes the request/response nature of an HTTP connection, specific HTTP versions might have different ways of mapping its semantics into the protocol's wire format."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2639]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "CONNECT is intended for use in requests to a proxy. The recipient can establish a tunnel either by directly connecting to the server identified by the request target or, if configured to use another proxy, by forwarding the CONNECT request to the next inbound proxy. An origin server MAY accept a CONNECT request, but most origin servers do not implement CONNECT."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2640]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Any "
                - link "2xx (Successful)" [ref=e2641]
                - StaticText " response indicates that the sender (and all inbound proxies) will switch to tunnel mode immediately after the response header section; data received after that header section is from the server identified by the request target. Any response other than a successful response indicates that the tunnel has not yet been formed."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2642]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A tunnel is closed when a tunnel intermediary detects that either side has closed its connection: the intermediary MUST attempt to send any outstanding data that came from the closed side to the other side, close both connections, and then discard any remaining data left undelivered."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2643]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Proxy authentication might be used to establish the authority to create a tunnel. For example,"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2644]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3874]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "CONNECT server.example.com:443 HTTP/1.1\nHost: server.example.com:443\nProxy-Authorization: basic aGVsbG86d29ybGQ=\n\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2645]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "There are significant risks in establishing a tunnel to arbitrary servers, particularly when the destination is a well-known or reserved TCP port that is not intended for Web traffic. For example, a CONNECT to \"example.com:25\" would suggest that the proxy connect to the reserved port for SMTP traffic; if allowed, that could trick the proxy into relaying spam email. Proxies that support CONNECT SHOULD restrict its use to a limited set of known ports or a configurable list of safe request targets."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2646]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A server MUST NOT send any Transfer-Encoding or "
                - link "Content-Length" [ref=e2647]
                - StaticText " header fields in a "
                - link "2xx (Successful)" [ref=e2648]
                - StaticText " response to CONNECT. A client MUST ignore any Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header fields received in a successful response to CONNECT."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2649]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A CONNECT request message does not have content. The interpretation of data sent after the header section of the CONNECT request message is specific to the version of HTTP in use."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2650]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Responses to the CONNECT method are not cacheable."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2651]
            - generic
              - heading "9.3.7. OPTIONS" [level=4, ref=e1826]
                - link "9.3.7. " [ref=e2652]
                - link "OPTIONS" [ref=e2653]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The OPTIONS method requests information about the communication options available for the target resource, at either the origin server or an intervening intermediary. This method allows a client to determine the options and/or requirements associated with a resource, or the capabilities of a server, without implying a resource action."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2654]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An OPTIONS request with an asterisk (\"*\") as the request target ("
                - link "Section 7.1" [ref=e2655]
                - StaticText ") applies to the server in general rather than to a specific resource. Since a server's communication options typically depend on the resource, the \"*\" request is only useful as a \"ping\" or \"no-op\" type of method; it does nothing beyond allowing the client to test the capabilities of the server. For example, this can be used to test a proxy for HTTP/1.1 conformance (or lack thereof)."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2656]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "If the request target is not an asterisk, the OPTIONS request applies to the options that are available when communicating with the target resource."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2657]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A server generating a successful response to OPTIONS SHOULD send any header that might indicate optional features implemented by the server and applicable to the target resource (e.g., "
                - link "Allow" [ref=e2658]
                - StaticText "), including potential extensions not defined by this specification. The response content, if any, might also describe the communication options in a machine or human-readable representation. A standard format for such a representation is not defined by this specification, but might be defined by future extensions to HTTP."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2659]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A client MAY send a "
                - link "Max-Forwards" [ref=e2660]
                - StaticText " header field in an OPTIONS request to target a specific recipient in the request chain (see "
                - link "Section 7.6.2" [ref=e2661]
                - StaticText "). A proxy MUST NOT generate a Max-Forwards header field while forwarding a request unless that request was received with a Max-Forwards field."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2662]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A client that generates an OPTIONS request containing content MUST send a valid "
                - link "Content-Type" [ref=e2663]
                - StaticText " header field describing the representation media type. Note that this specification does not define any use for such content."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2664]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Responses to the OPTIONS method are not cacheable."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2665]
            - generic
              - heading "9.3.8. TRACE" [level=4, ref=e1827]
                - link "9.3.8. " [ref=e2666]
                - link "TRACE" [ref=e2667]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The TRACE method requests a remote, application-level loop-back of the request message. The final recipient of the request SHOULD reflect the message received, excluding some fields described below, back to the client as the content of a "
                - link "200 (OK)" [ref=e2668]
                - StaticText " response. The \"message/http\" format ("
                - link "Section 10.1" [expanded=false, ref=e2669]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "HTTP/1.1" [ref=e2670]
                - StaticText "]) is one way to do so. The final recipient is either the origin server or the first server to receive a "
                - link "Max-Forwards" [ref=e2671]
                - StaticText " value of zero (0) in the request ("
                - link "Section 7.6.2" [ref=e2672]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2673]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A client MUST NOT generate fields in a TRACE request containing sensitive data that might be disclosed by the response. For example, it would be foolish for a user agent to send stored user credentials ("
                - link "Section 11" [ref=e2674]
                - StaticText ") or cookies ["
                - link "COOKIE" [ref=e2675]
                - StaticText "] in a TRACE request. The final recipient of the request SHOULD exclude any request fields that are likely to contain sensitive data when that recipient generates the response content."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2676]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "TRACE allows the client to see what is being received at the other end of the request chain and use that data for testing or diagnostic information. The value of the "
                - link "Via" [ref=e2677]
                - StaticText " header field ("
                - link "Section 7.6.3" [ref=e2678]
                - StaticText ") is of particular interest, since it acts as a trace of the request chain. Use of the "
                - link "Max-Forwards" [ref=e2679]
                - StaticText " header field allows the client to limit the length of the request chain, which is useful for testing a chain of proxies forwarding messages in an infinite loop."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2680]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A client MUST NOT send content in a TRACE request."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2681]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Responses to the TRACE method are not cacheable."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2682]

            - heading "10.1. Request Context Fields" [level=3, ref=e287]
              - link "10.1. " [ref=e1037]
              - link "Request Context Fields" [ref=e1038]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The request header fields below provide additional information about the request context, including information about the user, user agent, and resource behind the request."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1039]
            - generic
              - heading "10.1.1. Expect" [level=4, ref=e1828]
                - link "10.1.1. " [ref=e2683]
                - link "Expect" [ref=e2684]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Expect\" header field in a request indicates a certain set of behaviors (expectations) that need to be supported by the server in order to properly handle this request."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2685]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3875]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Expect =      #expectation\n  expectation = token [ \"=\" ( token / quoted-string ) parameters ]\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2686]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The Expect field value is case-insensitive."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2687]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The only expectation defined by this specification is \"100-continue\" (with no defined parameters)."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2688]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A server that receives an Expect field value containing a member other than "
                - link "100-continue" [ref=e2689]
                - StaticText " MAY respond with a "
                - link "417 (Expectation Failed)" [ref=e2690]
                - StaticText " status code to indicate that the unexpected expectation cannot be met."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2691]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A \"100-continue\" expectation informs recipients that the client is about to send (presumably large) content in this request and wishes to receive a "
                - link "100 (Continue)" [ref=e2692]
                - StaticText " interim response if the method, target URI, and header fields are not sufficient to cause an immediate success, redirect, or error response. This allows the client to wait for an indication that it is worthwhile to send the content before actually doing so, which can improve efficiency when the data is huge or when the client anticipates that an error is likely (e.g., when sending a state-changing method, for the first time, without previously verified authentication credentials)."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2693]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For example, a request that begins with"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2694]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3876]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "PUT /somewhere/fun HTTP/1.1\nHost: origin.example.com\nContent-Type: video/h264\nContent-Length: 1234567890987\nExpect: 100-continue\n\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2695]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "allows the origin server to immediately respond with an error message, such as "
                - link "401 (Unauthorized)" [ref=e2696]
                - StaticText " or "
                - link "405 (Method Not Allowed)" [ref=e2697]
                - StaticText ", before the client starts filling the pipes with an unnecessary data transfer."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2698]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Requirements for clients:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2699]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "A client MUST NOT generate a 100-continue expectation in a request that does not include content."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3877]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "A client that will wait for a "
                  - link "100 (Continue)" [ref=e3878]
                  - StaticText " response before sending the request content MUST send an "
                  - link "Expect" [ref=e3879]
                  - StaticText " header field containing a 100-continue expectation."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3880]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "A client that sends a 100-continue expectation is not required to wait for any specific length of time; such a client MAY proceed to send the content even if it has not yet received a response. Furthermore, since "
                  - link "100 (Continue)" [ref=e3881]
                  - StaticText " responses cannot be sent through an HTTP/1.0 intermediary, such a client SHOULD NOT wait for an indefinite period before sending the content."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3882]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "A client that receives a "
                  - link "417 (Expectation Failed)" [ref=e3883]
                  - StaticText " status code in response to a request containing a 100-continue expectation SHOULD repeat that request without a 100-continue expectation, since the 417 response merely indicates that the response chain does not support expectations (e.g., it passes through an HTTP/1.0 server)."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3884]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Requirements for servers:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2700]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "A server that receives a 100-continue expectation in an HTTP/1.0 request MUST ignore that expectation."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3885]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "A server MAY omit sending a "
                  - link "100 (Continue)" [ref=e3886]
                  - StaticText " response if it has already received some or all of the content for the corresponding request, or if the framing indicates that there is no content."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3887]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "A server that sends a "
                  - link "100 (Continue)" [ref=e3888]
                  - StaticText " response MUST ultimately send a final status code, once it receives and processes the request content, unless the connection is closed prematurely."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3889]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "A server that responds with a final status code before reading the entire request content SHOULD indicate whether it intends to close the connection (e.g., see "
                  - link "Section 9.6" [expanded=false, ref=e3890]
                  - StaticText " of ["
                  - link "HTTP/1.1" [ref=e3891]
                  - StaticText "]) or continue reading the request content."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3892]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Upon receiving an HTTP/1.1 (or later) request that has a method, target URI, and complete header section that contains a 100-continue expectation and an indication that request content will follow, an origin server MUST send either:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2701]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "an immediate response with a final status code, if that status can be determined by examining just the method, target URI, and header fields, or"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3893]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "an immediate "
                  - link "100 (Continue)" [ref=e3894]
                  - StaticText " response to encourage the client to send the request content."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3895]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The origin server MUST NOT wait for the content before sending the "
                - link "100 (Continue)" [ref=e2702]
                - StaticText " response."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2703]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Upon receiving an HTTP/1.1 (or later) request that has a method, target URI, and complete header section that contains a 100-continue expectation and indicates a request content will follow, a proxy MUST either:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2704]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "send an immediate response with a final status code, if that status can be determined by examining just the method, target URI, and header fields, or"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3896]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "forward the request toward the origin server by sending a corresponding request-line and header section to the next inbound server."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3897]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "If the proxy believes (from configuration or past interaction) that the next inbound server only supports HTTP/1.0, the proxy MAY generate an immediate "
                - link "100 (Continue)" [ref=e2705]
                - StaticText " response to encourage the client to begin sending the content."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2706]

              - heading "10.1.2. From" [level=4, ref=e1829]
                - link "10.1.2. " [ref=e2707]
                - link "From" [ref=e2708]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"From\" header field contains an Internet email address for a human user who controls the requesting user agent. The address ought to be machine-usable, as defined by \"mailbox\" in "
                - link "Section 3.4" [expanded=false, ref=e2709]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "RFC5322" [expanded=false, ref=e2710]
                - StaticText "]:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2711]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3898]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  From    = mailbox\n\n  mailbox = <mailbox, see [RFC5322], Section 3.4>\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2712]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An example is:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2713]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3899]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "From: spider-admin@example.org\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2714]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The From header field is rarely sent by non-robotic user agents. A user agent SHOULD NOT send a From header field without explicit configuration by the user, since that might conflict with the user's privacy interests or their site's security policy."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2715]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A robotic user agent SHOULD send a valid From header field so that the person responsible for running the robot can be contacted if problems occur on servers, such as if the robot is sending excessive, unwanted, or invalid requests."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2716]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A server SHOULD NOT use the From header field for access control or authentication, since its value is expected to be visible to anyone receiving or observing the request and is often recorded within logfiles and error reports without any expectation of privacy."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2717]
            - generic
              - heading "10.1.3. Referer" [level=4, ref=e1830]
                - link "10.1.3. " [ref=e2718]
                - link "Referer" [ref=e2719]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Referer\" [sic] header field allows the user agent to specify a URI reference for the resource from which the "
                - link "target URI" [ref=e2720]
                - StaticText " was obtained (i.e., the \"referrer\", though the field name is misspelled). A user agent MUST NOT include the fragment and userinfo components of the URI reference ["
                - link "URI" [ref=e2721]
                - StaticText "], if any, when generating the Referer field value."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2722]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3900]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Referer = absolute-URI / partial-URI\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2723]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The field value is either an "
                - link "absolute-URI" [ref=e2724]
                - StaticText " or a "
                - link "partial-URI" [ref=e2725]
                - StaticText ". In the latter case ("
                - link "Section 4" [ref=e2726]
                - StaticText "), the referenced URI is relative to the target URI (["
                - link "URI" [ref=e2727]
                - StaticText "], "
                - link "Section 5" [expanded=false, ref=e2728]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2729]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The Referer header field allows servers to generate back-links to other resources for simple analytics, logging, optimized caching, etc. It also allows obsolete or mistyped links to be found for maintenance. Some servers use the Referer header field as a means of denying links from other sites (so-called \"deep linking\") or restricting cross-site request forgery (CSRF), but not all requests contain it."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2730]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Example:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2731]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3901]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "Referer: http://www.example.org/hypertext/Overview.html\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2732]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "If the target URI was obtained from a source that does not have its own URI (e.g., input from the user keyboard, or an entry within the user's bookmarks/favorites), the user agent MUST either exclude the Referer header field or send it with a value of \"about:blank\"."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2733]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The Referer header field value need not convey the full URI of the referring resource; a user agent MAY truncate parts other than the referring origin."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2734]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The Referer header field has the potential to reveal information about the request context or browsing history of the user, which is a privacy concern if the referring resource's identifier reveals personal information (such as an account name) or a resource that is supposed to be confidential (such as behind a firewall or internal to a secured service). Most general-purpose user agents do not send the Referer header field when the referring resource is a local \"file\" or \"data\" URI. A user agent SHOULD NOT send a "
                - link "Referer" [ref=e2735]
                - StaticText " header field if the referring resource was accessed with a secure protocol and the request target has an origin differing from that of the referring resource, unless the referring resource explicitly allows Referer to be sent. A user agent MUST NOT send a "
                - link "Referer" [ref=e2736]
                - StaticText " header field in an unsecured HTTP request if the referring resource was accessed with a secure protocol. See "
                - link "Section 17.9" [ref=e2737]
                - StaticText " for additional security considerations."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2738]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Some intermediaries have been known to indiscriminately remove Referer header fields from outgoing requests. This has the unfortunate side effect of interfering with protection against CSRF attacks, which can be far more harmful to their users. Intermediaries and user agent extensions that wish to limit information disclosure in Referer ought to restrict their changes to specific edits, such as replacing internal domain names with pseudonyms or truncating the query and/or path components. An intermediary SHOULD NOT modify or delete the Referer header field when the field value shares the same scheme and host as the target URI."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2739]
            - generic
              - heading "10.1.4. TE" [level=4, ref=e1831]
                - link "10.1.4. " [ref=e2740]
                - link "TE" [ref=e2741]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"TE\" header field describes capabilities of the client with regard to transfer codings and trailer sections."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2742]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "As described in "
                - link "Section 6.5" [ref=e2743]
                - StaticText ", a TE field with a \"trailers\" member sent in a request indicates that the client will not discard trailer fields."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2744]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "TE is also used within HTTP/1.1 to advise servers about which transfer codings the client is able to accept in a response. As of publication, only HTTP/1.1 uses transfer codings (see "
                - link "Section 7" [expanded=false, ref=e2745]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "HTTP/1.1" [ref=e2746]
                - StaticText "])."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2747]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The TE field value is a list of members, with each member (aside from \"trailers\") consisting of a transfer coding name token with an optional weight indicating the client's relative preference for that transfer coding ("
                - link "Section 12.4.2" [ref=e2748]
                - StaticText ") and optional parameters for that transfer coding."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2749]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3902]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  TE                 = #t-codings\n  t-codings          = \"trailers\" / ( transfer-coding [ weight ] )\n  transfer-coding    = token *( OWS \";\" OWS transfer-parameter )\n  transfer-parameter = token BWS \"=\" BWS ( token / quoted-string )\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2750]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A sender of TE MUST also send a \"TE\" connection option within the "

              - heading "10.1.5. User-Agent" [level=4, ref=e1832]
                - link "10.1.5. " [ref=e2754]
                - link "User-Agent" [ref=e2755]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"User-Agent\" header field contains information about the user agent originating the request, which is often used by servers to help identify the scope of reported interoperability problems, to work around or tailor responses to avoid particular user agent limitations, and for analytics regarding browser or operating system use. A user agent SHOULD send a User-Agent header field in each request unless specifically configured not to do so."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2756]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3903]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  User-Agent = product *( RWS ( product / comment ) )\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2757]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The User-Agent field value consists of one or more product identifiers, each followed by zero or more comments ("
                - link "Section 5.6.5" [ref=e2758]
                - StaticText "), which together identify the user agent software and its significant subproducts. By convention, the product identifiers are listed in decreasing order of their significance for identifying the user agent software. Each product identifier consists of a name and optional version."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2759]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3904]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  product         = token [\"/\" product-version]\n  product-version = token\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2760]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A sender SHOULD limit generated product identifiers to what is necessary to identify the product; a sender MUST NOT generate advertising or other nonessential information within the product identifier. A sender SHOULD NOT generate information in "
                - link "product-version" [ref=e2761]
                  - StaticText "product-version"
                - StaticText " that is not a version identifier (i.e., successive versions of the same product name ought to differ only in the product-version portion of the product identifier)."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2762]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Example:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2763]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3905]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "User-Agent: CERN-LineMode/2.15 libwww/2.17b3\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2764]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A user agent SHOULD NOT generate a User-Agent header field containing needlessly fine-grained detail and SHOULD limit the addition of subproducts by third parties. Overly long and detailed User-Agent field values increase request latency and the risk of a user being identified against their wishes (\"fingerprinting\")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2765]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Likewise, implementations are encouraged not to use the product tokens of other implementations in order to declare compatibility with them, as this circumvents the purpose of the field. If a user agent masquerades as a different user agent, recipients can assume that the user intentionally desires to see responses tailored for that identified user agent, even if they might not work as well for the actual user agent being used."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2766]
          - generic
            - heading "10.2. Response Context Fields" [level=3, ref=e288]
              - link "10.2. " [ref=e1040]
              - link "Response Context Fields" [ref=e1041]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The response header fields below provide additional information about the response, beyond what is implied by the status code, including information about the server, about the "
              - link "target resource" [ref=e1042]
              - StaticText ", or about related resources."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1043]
            - generic
              - heading "10.2.1. Allow" [level=4, ref=e1833]
                - link "10.2.1. " [ref=e2767]
                - link "Allow" [ref=e2768]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Allow\" header field lists the set of methods advertised as supported by the "
                - link "target resource" [ref=e2769]
                - StaticText ". The purpose of this field is strictly to inform the recipient of valid request methods associated with the resource."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2770]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3906]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Allow = #method\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2771]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Example of use:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2772]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3907]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "Allow: GET, HEAD, PUT\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2773]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The actual set of allowed methods is defined by the origin server at the time of each request. An origin server MUST generate an Allow header field in a "
                - link "405 (Method Not Allowed)" [ref=e2774]
                - StaticText " response and MAY do so in any other response. An empty Allow field value indicates that the resource allows no methods, which might occur in a 405 response if the resource has been temporarily disabled by configuration."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2775]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A proxy MUST NOT modify the Allow header field -- it does not need to understand all of the indicated methods in order to handle them according to the generic message handling rules."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2776]
            - generic
              - heading "10.2.2. Location" [level=4, ref=e1834]
                - link "10.2.2. " [ref=e2777]
                - link "Location" [ref=e2778]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Location\" header field is used in some responses to refer to a specific resource in relation to the response. The type of relationship is defined by the combination of request method and status code semantics."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2779]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3908]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Location = URI-reference\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2780]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The field value consists of a single URI-reference. When it has the form of a relative reference (["
                - link "URI" [ref=e2781]
                - StaticText "], "
                - link "Section 4.2" [expanded=false, ref=e2782]
                - StaticText "), the final value is computed by resolving it against the target URI (["
                - link "URI" [ref=e2783]
                - StaticText "], "
                - link "Section 5" [expanded=false, ref=e2784]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2785]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For "
                - link "201 (Created)" [ref=e2786]
                - StaticText " responses, the Location value refers to the primary resource created by the request. For "
                - link "3xx (Redirection)" [ref=e2787]
                - StaticText " responses, the Location value refers to the preferred target resource for automatically redirecting the request."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2788]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "If the Location value provided in a "
                - link "3xx (Redirection)" [ref=e2789]
                - StaticText " response does not have a fragment component, a user agent MUST process the redirection as if the value inherits the fragment component of the URI reference used to generate the target URI (i.e., the redirection inherits the original reference's fragment, if any)."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2790]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For example, a GET request generated for the URI reference \"http://www.example.org/~tim\" might result in a "

                - StaticText " Some recipients attempt to recover from Location header fields that are not valid URI references. If an invalid message is sent with multiple Location field lines, a recipient along the path might combine those field lines into one value.               - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Server\" header field contains information about the software used by the origin server to handle the request, which is often used by clients to help identify the scope of reported interoperability problems, to work around or tailor requests to avoid particular server limitations, and for analytics regarding server or operating system use.                 - link "¶" [ref=e2814]

                - StaticText "The Server header field value consists of one or more product identifiers, each followed by zero or more comments ("
                - link "Section 5.6.5" [ref=e2816]
                - StaticText "), which together identify the origin server software and its significant subproducts.                 - link "Section 10.1.5" [ref=e2817]
                - StaticText "."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2818]

                - StaticText "Example:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2819]

                - link "¶" [ref=e2820]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An origin server SHOULD NOT generate a Server header field containing needlessly fine-grained detail and SHOULD limit the addition of subproducts by third parties.             - heading "11.5. Establishing a Protection Space (Realm)" [level=3, ref=e293]
              - link "11.5. " [ref=e1097]
              - link "Establishing a Protection Space (Realm)" [ref=e1098]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The \"realm\" authentication parameter is reserved for use by authentication schemes that wish to indicate a scope of protection."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1099]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A \"protection space\" is defined by the origin (see "
              - link "Section 4.3.1" [ref=e1100]
              - StaticText ") of the server being accessed, in combination with the realm value if present. These realms allow the protected resources on a server to be partitioned into a set of protection spaces, each with its own authentication scheme and/or authorization database. The realm value is a string, generally assigned by the origin server, that can have additional semantics specific to the authentication scheme. Note that a response can have multiple challenges with the same auth-scheme but with different realms."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1101]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The protection space determines the domain over which credentials can be automatically applied. If a prior request has been authorized, the user agent MAY reuse the same credentials for all other requests within that protection space for a period of time determined by the authentication scheme, parameters, and/or user preferences (such as a configurable inactivity timeout)."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1102]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The extent of a protection space, and therefore the requests to which credentials might be automatically applied, is not necessarily known to clients without additional information. An authentication scheme might define parameters that describe the extent of a protection space. Unless specifically allowed by the authentication scheme, a single protection space cannot extend outside the scope of its server."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1103]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "For historical reasons, a sender MUST only generate the quoted-string syntax. Recipients might have to support both token and quoted-string syntax for maximum interoperability with existing clients that have been accepting both notations for a long time."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1104]

                - StaticText "The \"Proxy-Authenticate\" header field consists of at least one challenge that indicates the authentication scheme(s) and parameters applicable to the proxy for this request. A proxy MUST send at least one Proxy-Authenticate header field in each "

                - StaticText "Unlike "
                - link "WWW-Authenticate" [ref=e2864]
                  - StaticText "WWW-Authenticate"
                - StaticText ", the Proxy-Authenticate header field applies only to the next outbound client on the response chain. This is because only the client that chose a given proxy is likely to have the credentials necessary for authentication.               - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Proxy-Authorization\" header field allows the client to identify itself (or its user) to a proxy that requires authentication. Its value consists of credentials containing the authentication information of the client for the proxy and/or realm of the resource being requested."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2871]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3927]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Proxy-Authorization = credentials\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2872]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Unlike "
                - link "Authorization" [ref=e2873]
                - StaticText ", the Proxy-Authorization header field applies only to the next inbound proxy that demanded authentication using the "
                - link "Proxy-Authenticate" [ref=e2874]
                  - StaticText "Proxy-Authenticate"
                - StaticText " header field. When multiple proxies are used in a chain, the Proxy-Authorization header field is consumed by the first inbound proxy that was expecting to receive credentials. A proxy MAY relay the credentials from the client request to the next proxy if that is the mechanism by which the proxies cooperatively authenticate a given request."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2875]
            - generic
              - heading "11.7.3. Proxy-Authentication-Info" [level=4, ref=e1848]
                - link "11.7.3. " [ref=e2876]
                - link "Proxy-Authentication-Info" [ref=e2877]
                  - StaticText "Proxy-Authentication-Info"
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Proxy-Authentication-Info\" response header field is equivalent to "
                - link "Authentication-Info" [ref=e2878]
                  - StaticText "Authentication-Info"
                - StaticText ", except that it applies to proxy authentication ("
                - link "Section 11.3" [ref=e2879]
                - StaticText ") and its semantics are defined by the authentication scheme indicated by the Proxy-Authorization header field ("
                - link "Section 11.7.2" [ref=e2880]

                - link "¶" [ref=e2881]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3928]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Proxy-Authentication-Info = #auth-param\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2882]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "However, unlike "
                - link "Authentication-Info" [ref=e2883]
                  - StaticText "Authentication-Info"
                - StaticText ", the Proxy-Authentication-Info header field applies only to the next outbound client on the response chain. This is because only the client that chose a given proxy is likely to have the credentials necessary for authentication. However, when multiple proxies are used within the same administrative domain, such as office and regional caching proxies within a large corporate network, it is common for credentials to be generated by the user agent and passed through the hierarchy until consumed. Hence, in such a configuration, it will appear as if Proxy-Authentication-Info is being forwarded because each proxy will send the same field value."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2884]

        - generic
          - heading "12. Content Negotiation" [level=2, ref=e38]
            - link "12. " [ref=e115]
            - link "Content Negotiation" [ref=e116]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "When responses convey content, whether indicating a success or an error, the origin server often has different ways of representing that information; for example, in different formats, languages, or encodings. Likewise, different users or user agents might have differing capabilities, characteristics, or preferences that could influence which representation, among those available, would be best to deliver. For this reason, HTTP provides mechanisms for "
            - link "content negotiation" [ref=e117]
            - StaticText "."
            - link "¶" [ref=e118]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "This specification defines three patterns of content negotiation that can be made visible within the protocol: \"proactive\" negotiation, where the server selects the representation based upon the user agent's stated preferences; \"reactive\" negotiation, where the server provides a list of representations for the user agent to choose from; and \"request content\" negotiation, where the user agent selects the representation for a future request based upon the server's stated preferences in past responses."
            - link "¶" [ref=e119]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Other patterns of content negotiation include \"conditional content\", where the representation consists of multiple parts that are selectively rendered based on user agent parameters, \"active content\", where the representation contains a script that makes additional (more specific) requests based on the user agent characteristics, and \"Transparent Content Negotiation\" (["
            - link "RFC2295" [expanded=false, ref=e120]
            - StaticText "]), where content selection is performed by an intermediary. These patterns are not mutually exclusive, and each has trade-offs in applicability and practicality."
            - link "¶" [ref=e121]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Note that, in all cases, HTTP is not aware of the resource semantics. The consistency with which an origin server responds to requests, over time and over the varying dimensions of content negotiation, and thus the \"sameness\" of a resource's observed representations over time, is determined entirely by whatever entity or algorithm selects or generates those responses."
            - link "¶" [ref=e122]
          - generic
            - heading "12.1. Proactive Negotiation" [level=3, ref=e296]
              - link "12.1. " [ref=e1109]
              - link "Proactive Negotiation" [ref=e1110]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "When content negotiation preferences are sent by the user agent in a request to encourage an algorithm located at the server to select the preferred representation, it is called \"proactive negotiation\" (a.k.a., \"server-driven negotiation\"). Selection is based on the available representations for a response (the dimensions over which it might vary, such as language, content coding, etc.) compared to various information supplied in the request, including both the explicit negotiation header fields below and implicit characteristics, such as the client's network address or parts of the "
              - link "User-Agent" [ref=e1111]
              - StaticText " field."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1112]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Proactive negotiation is advantageous when the algorithm for selecting from among the available representations is difficult to describe to a user agent, or when the server desires to send its \"best guess\" to the user agent along with the first response (when that \"best guess\" is good enough for the user, this avoids the round-trip delay of a subsequent request). In order to improve the server's guess, a user agent MAY send request header fields that describe its preferences."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1113]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Proactive negotiation has serious disadvantages:"
              - link "¶" [ref=e1114]
            - list
              - listitem [level=1]
                - ListMarker "• "
                - StaticText "It is impossible for the server to accurately determine what might be \"best\" for any given user, since that would require complete knowledge of both the capabilities of the user agent and the intended use for the response (e.g., does the user want to view it on screen or print it on paper?);"
                - link "¶" [ref=e1849]
              - listitem [level=1]
                - ListMarker "• "
                - StaticText "Having the user agent describe its capabilities in every request can be both very inefficient (given that only a small percentage of responses have multiple representations) and a potential risk to the user's privacy;"
                - link "¶" [ref=e1850]
              - listitem [level=1]
                - ListMarker "• "
                - StaticText "It complicates the implementation of an origin server and the algorithms for generating responses to a request; and,"
                - link "¶" [ref=e1851]
              - listitem [level=1]
                - ListMarker "• "
                - StaticText "It limits the reusability of responses for shared caching."
                - link "¶" [ref=e1852]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A user agent cannot rely on proactive negotiation preferences being consistently honored, since the origin server might not implement proactive negotiation for the requested resource or might decide that sending a response that doesn't conform to the user agent's preferences is better than sending a "
              - link "406 (Not Acceptable)" [ref=e1115]
              - StaticText " response."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1116]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A "
              - link "Vary" [ref=e1117]
              - StaticText " header field ("
              - link "Section 12.5.5" [ref=e1118]
              - StaticText ") is often sent in a response subject to proactive negotiation to indicate what parts of the request information were used in the selection algorithm."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1119]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The request header fields "
              - link "Accept" [ref=e1120]
              - StaticText ", "
              - link "Accept-Charset" [ref=e1121]
              - StaticText ", "
              - link "Accept-Encoding" [ref=e1122]
                - StaticText "Accept-Encoding"
              - StaticText ", and "
              - link "Accept-Language" [ref=e1123]
                - StaticText "Accept-Language"
              - StaticText " are defined below for a user agent to engage in "
              - link "proactive negotiation" [ref=e1124]
              - StaticText " of the response content. The preferences sent in these fields apply to any content in the response, including representations of the target resource, representations of error or processing status, and potentially even the miscellaneous text strings that might appear within the protocol."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1125]
          - generic
            - heading "12.2. Reactive Negotiation" [level=3, ref=e297]
              - link "12.2. " [ref=e1126]
              - link "Reactive Negotiation" [ref=e1127]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "With \"reactive negotiation\" (a.k.a., \"agent-driven negotiation\"), selection of content (regardless of the status code) is performed by the user agent after receiving an initial response. The mechanism for reactive negotiation might be as simple as a list of references to alternative representations."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1128]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "If the user agent is not satisfied by the initial response content, it can perform a GET request on one or more of the alternative resources to obtain a different representation. Selection of such alternatives might be performed automatically (by the user agent) or manually (e.g., by the user selecting from a hypertext menu)."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1129]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server might choose not to send an initial representation, other than the list of alternatives, and thereby indicate that reactive negotiation by the user agent is preferred. For example, the alternatives listed in responses with the "
              - link "300 (Multiple Choices)" [ref=e1130]
              - StaticText " and "
              - link "406 (Not Acceptable)" [ref=e1131]
              - StaticText " status codes include information about available representations so that the user or user agent can react by making a selection."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1132]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Reactive negotiation is advantageous when the response would vary over commonly used dimensions (such as type, language, or encoding), when the origin server is unable to determine a user agent's capabilities from examining the request, and generally when public caches are used to distribute server load and reduce network usage."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1133]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Reactive negotiation suffers from the disadvantages of transmitting a list of alternatives to the user agent, which degrades user-perceived latency if transmitted in the header section, and needing a second request to obtain an alternate representation. Furthermore, this specification does not define a mechanism for supporting automatic selection, though it does not prevent such a mechanism from being developed."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1134]
          - generic
            - heading "12.3. Request Content Negotiation" [level=3, ref=e298]
              - link "12.3. " [ref=e1135]
              - link "Request Content Negotiation" [ref=e1136]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "When content negotiation preferences are sent in a server's response, the listed preferences are called \"request content negotiation\" because they intend to influence selection of an appropriate content for subsequent requests to that resource. For example, the "

              - StaticText " ("
              - link "Section 12.5.1" [ref=e1138]

                - StaticText "Accept-Encoding"
              - StaticText " ("
              - link "Section 12.5.3" [ref=e1140]
              - StaticText ") header fields can be sent in a response to indicate preferred media types and content codings for subsequent requests to that resource."

              - StaticText "Similarly, "

                - link "12.4.1. " [ref=e2887]
                - link "Absence" [ref=e2888]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For each of the content negotiation fields, a request that does not contain the field implies that the sender has no preference on that dimension of negotiation."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2889]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "If a content negotiation header field is present in a request and none of the available representations for the response can be considered acceptable according to it, the origin server can either honor the header field by sending a "
                - link "406 (Not Acceptable)" [ref=e2890]
                - StaticText " response or disregard the header field by treating the response as if it is not subject to content negotiation for that request header field. This does not imply, however, that the client will be able to use the representation."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2891]
              - paragraph
                - strong
                  - StaticText "Note:"
                - StaticText " A user agent sending these header fields makes it easier for a server to identify an individual by virtue of the user agent's request characteristics ("
                - link "Section 17.13" [ref=e3929]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3930]
            - generic
              - heading "12.4.2. Quality Values" [level=4, ref=e1854]
                - link "12.4.2. " [ref=e2892]
                - link "Quality Values" [ref=e2893]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The content negotiation fields defined by this specification use a common parameter, named \"q\" (case-insensitive), to assign a relative \"weight\" to the preference for that associated kind of content. This weight is referred to as a \"quality value\" (or \"qvalue\") because the same parameter name is often used within server configurations to assign a weight to the relative quality of the various representations that can be selected for a resource."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2894]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The weight is normalized to a real number in the range 0 through 1, where 0.001 is the least preferred and 1 is the most preferred; a value of 0 means \"not acceptable\". If no \"q\" parameter is present, the default weight is 1."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2895]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3931]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  weight = OWS \";\" OWS \"q=\" qvalue\n  qvalue = ( \"0\" [ \".\" 0*3DIGIT ] )\n         / ( \"1\" [ \".\" 0*3(\"0\") ] )\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2896]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A sender of qvalue MUST NOT generate more than three digits after the decimal point. User configuration of these values ought to be limited in the same fashion."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2897]
            - generic
              - heading "12.4.3. Wildcard Values" [level=4, ref=e1855]
                - link "12.4.3. " [ref=e2898]
                - link "Wildcard Values" [ref=e2899]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Most of these header fields, where indicated, define a wildcard value (\"*\") to select unspecified values. If no wildcard is present, values that are not explicitly mentioned in the field are considered unacceptable. Within "
                - link "Vary" [ref=e2900]
                - StaticText ", the wildcard value means that the variance is unlimited."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2901]
              - paragraph
                - strong
                  - StaticText "Note:"
                - StaticText " In practice, using wildcards in content negotiation has limited practical value because it is seldom useful to say, for example, \"I prefer image/* more or less than (some other specific value)\". By sending Accept: */*;q=0, clients can explicitly request a "
                - link "406 (Not Acceptable)" [ref=e3932]
                - StaticText " response if a more preferred format is not available, but they still need to be able to handle a different response since the server is allowed to ignore their preference."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3933]

            - heading "12.5. Content Negotiation Fields" [level=3, ref=e300]
              - link "12.5. " [ref=e1147]

            - generic
              - heading "12.5.1. Accept" [level=4, ref=e1856]
                - link "12.5.1. " [ref=e2902]
                - link "Accept" [ref=e2903]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Accept\" header field can be used by user agents to specify their preferences regarding response media types. For example, Accept header fields can be used to indicate that the request is specifically limited to a small set of desired types, as in the case of a request for an in-line image."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2904]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "When sent by a server in a response, Accept provides information about which content types are preferred in the content of a subsequent request to the same resource."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2905]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3934]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Accept = #( media-range [ weight ] )\n\n  media-range    = ( \"*/*\"\n                     / ( type \"/\" \"*\" )\n                     / ( type \"/\" subtype )\n                   ) parameters\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2906]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The asterisk \"*\" character is used to group media types into ranges, with \"*/*\" indicating all media types and \"type/*\" indicating all subtypes of that type. The media-range can include media type parameters that are applicable to that range."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2907]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Each media-range might be followed by optional applicable media type parameters (e.g., "
                - link "charset" [ref=e2908]
                - StaticText "), followed by an optional \"q\" parameter for indicating a relative weight ("
                - link "Section 12.4.2" [ref=e2909]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2910]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Previous specifications allowed additional extension parameters to appear after the weight parameter. The accept extension grammar (accept-params, accept-ext) has been removed because it had a complicated definition, was not being used in practice, and is more easily deployed through new header fields. Senders using weights SHOULD send \"q\" last (after all media-range parameters). Recipients SHOULD process any parameter named \"q\" as weight, regardless of parameter ordering."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2911]
              - paragraph
                - strong
                  - StaticText "Note:"
                - StaticText " Use of the \"q\" parameter name to control content negotiation would interfere with any media type parameter having the same name. Hence, the media type registry disallows parameters named \"q\"."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3935]

                  - StaticText "Accept-Encoding: compress, gzip\nAccept-Encoding:\nAccept-Encoding: *\nAccept-Encoding: compress;q=0.5, gzip;q=1.0\nAccept-Encoding: gzip;q=1.0, identity; q=0.5, *;q=0\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2945]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A server tests whether a content coding for a given representation is acceptable using these rules:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2946]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "1. "
                  - StaticText "If no Accept-Encoding header field is in the request, any content coding is considered acceptable by the user agent."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3951]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "2. "
                  - StaticText "If the representation has no content coding, then it is acceptable by default unless specifically excluded by the Accept-Encoding header field stating either \"identity;q=0\" or \"*;q=0\" without a more specific entry for \"identity\"."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3952]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "3. "
                  - StaticText "If the representation's content coding is one of the content codings listed in the Accept-Encoding field value, then it is acceptable unless it is accompanied by a qvalue of 0. (As defined in "
                  - link "Section 12.4.2" [ref=e3953]
                  - StaticText ", a qvalue of 0 means \"not acceptable\".)"
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3954]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A representation could be encoded with multiple content codings. However, most content codings are alternative ways to accomplish the same purpose (e.g., data compression). When selecting between multiple content codings that have the same purpose, the acceptable content coding with the highest non-zero qvalue is preferred."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2947]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An Accept-Encoding header field with a field value that is empty implies that the user agent does not want any content coding in response. If a non-empty Accept-Encoding header field is present in a request and none of the available representations for the response have a content coding that is listed as acceptable, the origin server SHOULD send a response without any content coding unless the identity coding is indicated as unacceptable."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2948]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "When the Accept-Encoding header field is present in a response, it indicates what content codings the resource was willing to accept in the associated request. The field value is evaluated the same way as in a request."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2949]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Note that this information is specific to the associated request; the set of supported encodings might be different for other resources on the same server and could change over time or depend on other aspects of the request (such as the request method)."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2950]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Servers that fail a request due to an unsupported content coding ought to respond with a "
                - link "415 (Unsupported Media Type)" [ref=e2951]
                - StaticText " status and include an Accept-Encoding header field in that response, allowing clients to distinguish between issues related to content codings and media types. In order to avoid confusion with issues related to media types, servers that fail a request with a 415 status for reasons unrelated to content codings MUST NOT include the Accept-Encoding header field."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2952]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The most common use of Accept-Encoding is in responses with a "
                - link "415 (Unsupported Media Type)" [ref=e2953]
                - StaticText " status code, in response to optimistic use of a content coding by clients. However, the header field can also be used to indicate to clients that content codings are supported in order to optimize future interactions. For example, a resource might include it in a "
                - link "2xx (Successful)" [ref=e2954]
                - StaticText " response when the request content was big enough to justify use of a compression coding but the client failed do so."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2955]

              - heading "12.5.5. Vary" [level=4, ref=e1860]
                - link "12.5.5. " [ref=e2978]

              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"Vary\" header field in a response describes what parts of a request message, aside from the method and target URI, might have influenced the origin server's process for selecting the content of this response."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2980]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3958]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  Vary = #( \"*\" / field-name )\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2981]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A Vary field value is either the wildcard member \"*\" or a list of request field names, known as the selecting header fields, that might have had a role in selecting the representation for this response. Potential selecting header fields are not limited to fields defined by this specification."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2982]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A list containing the member \"*\" signals that other aspects of the request might have played a role in selecting the response representation, possibly including aspects outside the message syntax (e.g., the client's network address). A recipient will not be able to determine whether this response is appropriate for a later request without forwarding the request to the origin server. A proxy MUST NOT generate \"*\" in a Vary field value."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2983]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For example, a response that contains"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2984]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3959]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "Vary: accept-encoding, accept-language\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2985]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "indicates that the origin server might have used the request's "
                - link "Accept-Encoding" [ref=e2986]
                  - StaticText "Accept-Encoding"
                - StaticText " and "
                - link "Accept-Language" [ref=e2987]
                  - StaticText "Accept-Language"
                - StaticText " header fields (or lack thereof) as determining factors while choosing the content for this response."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2988]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A Vary field containing a list of field names has two purposes:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e2989]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "1. "
                  - paragraph
                    - StaticText "To inform cache recipients that they MUST NOT use this response to satisfy a later request unless the later request has the same values for the listed header fields as the original request ("
                    - link "Section 4.1" [expanded=false, ref=e4765]
                    - StaticText " of ["
                    - link "CACHING" [ref=e4766]
                    - StaticText "]) or reuse of the response has been validated by the origin server. In other words, Vary expands the cache key required to match a new request to the stored cache entry."
                    - link "¶" [ref=e4767]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "2. "
                  - paragraph
                    - StaticText "To inform user agent recipients that this response was subject to content negotiation ("
                    - link "Section 12" [ref=e4768]
                    - StaticText ") and a different representation might be sent in a subsequent request if other values are provided in the listed header fields ("
                    - link "proactive negotiation" [ref=e4769]
                    - StaticText ")."
                    - link "¶" [ref=e4770]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An origin server SHOULD generate a Vary header field on a cacheable response when it wishes that response to be selectively reused for subsequent requests. Generally, that is the case when the response content has been tailored to better fit the preferences expressed by those selecting header fields, such as when an origin server has selected the response's language based on the request's "
                - link "Accept-Language" [ref=e2990]
                  - StaticText "Accept-Language"
                - StaticText " header field."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2991]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Vary might be elided when an origin server considers variance in content selection to be less significant than Vary's performance impact on caching, particularly when reuse is already limited by cache response directives ("
                - link "Section 5.2" [expanded=false, ref=e2992]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "CACHING" [ref=e2993]
                - StaticText "])."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2994]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "There is no need to send the Authorization field name in Vary because reuse of that response for a different user is prohibited by the field definition ("
                - link "Section 11.6.2" [ref=e2995]
                - StaticText "). Likewise, if the response content has been selected or influenced by network region, but the origin server wants the cached response to be reused even if recipients move from one region to another, then there is no need for the origin server to indicate such variance in Vary."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2996]
