          - heading "13. Conditional Requests" [level=2, ref=e39]
            - link "13. " [ref=e123]
            - link "Conditional Requests" [ref=e124]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "A conditional request is an HTTP request with one or more request header fields that indicate a precondition to be tested before applying the request method to the target resource. "
            - link "Section 13.2" [ref=e125]
            - StaticText " defines when to evaluate preconditions and their order of precedence when more than one precondition is present."
            - link "¶" [ref=e126]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Conditional GET requests are the most efficient mechanism for HTTP cache updates ["
            - link "CACHING" [ref=e127]
            - StaticText "]. Conditionals can also be applied to state-changing methods, such as PUT and DELETE, to prevent the \"lost update\" problem: one client accidentally overwriting the work of another client that has been acting in parallel."
            - link "¶" [ref=e128]
          - generic
            - heading "13.1. Preconditions" [level=3, ref=e301]
              - link "13.1. " [ref=e1149]
              - link "Preconditions" [ref=e1150]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Preconditions are usually defined with respect to a state of the target resource as a whole (its current value set) or the state as observed in a previously obtained representation (one value in that set). If a resource has multiple current representations, each with its own observable state, a precondition will assume that the mapping of each request to a "
              - link "selected representation" [ref=e1151]
              - StaticText " ("
              - link "Section 3.2" [ref=e1152]
              - StaticText ") is consistent over time. Regardless, if the mapping is inconsistent or the server is unable to select an appropriate representation, then no harm will result when the precondition evaluates to false."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1153]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Each precondition defined below consists of a comparison between a set of validators obtained from prior representations of the target resource to the current state of validators for the selected representation ("
              - link "Section 8.8" [ref=e1154]
              - StaticText "). Hence, these preconditions evaluate whether the state of the target resource has changed since a given state known by the client. The effect of such an evaluation depends on the method semantics and choice of conditional, as defined in "
              - link "Section 13.2" [ref=e1155]
              - StaticText "."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1156]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Other preconditions, defined by other specifications as extension fields, might place conditions on all recipients, on the state of the target resource in general, or on a group of resources. For instance, the \"If\" header field in WebDAV can make a request conditional on various aspects of multiple resources, such as locks, if the recipient understands and implements that field (["
              - link "WEBDAV" [ref=e1157]
              - StaticText "], "
              - link "Section 10.4" [expanded=false, ref=e1158]
              - StaticText ")."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1159]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Extensibility of preconditions is only possible when the precondition can be safely ignored if unknown (like "
              - link "If-Modified-Since" [ref=e1160]
                - StaticText "If-Modified-Since"
              - StaticText "), when deployment can be assumed for a given use case, or when implementation is signaled by some other property of the target resource. This encourages a focus on mutually agreed deployment of common standards."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1161]
            - generic
              - heading "13.1.1. If-Match" [level=4, ref=e1861]
                - link "13.1.1. " [ref=e2997]
                - link "If-Match" [ref=e2998]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The \"If-Match\" header field makes the request method conditional on the recipient origin server either having at least one current representation of the target resource, when the field value is \"*\", or having a current representation of the target resource that has an entity tag matching a member of the list of entity tags provided in the field value."
                - link "¶" [ref=e2999]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An origin server MUST use the strong comparison function when comparing entity tags for If-Match ("
                - link "Section 8.8.3.2" [ref=e3000]
                - StaticText "), since the client intends this precondition to prevent the method from being applied if there have been any changes to the representation data."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3001]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3960]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "  If-Match = \"*\" / #entity-tag\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3002]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Examples:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3003]
              - generic
                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e3961]
                  - status
                  - StaticText "If-Match: \"xyzzy\"\nIf-Match: \"xyzzy\", \"r2d2xxxx\", \"c3piozzzz\"\nIf-Match: *\n"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3004]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "If-Match is most often used with state-changing methods (e.g., POST, PUT, DELETE) to prevent accidental overwrites when multiple user agents might be acting in parallel on the same resource (i.e., to prevent the \"lost update\" problem). In general, it can be used with any method that involves the selection or modification of a representation to abort the request if the "
                - link "selected representation" [ref=e3005]
                - StaticText "'s current entity tag is not a member within the If-Match field value."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3006]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "When an origin server receives a request that selects a representation and that request includes an If-Match header field, the origin server MUST evaluate the If-Match condition per "
                - link "Section 13.2" [ref=e3007]
                - StaticText " prior to performing the method."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3008]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "To evaluate a received If-Match header field:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3009]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "1. "
                  - StaticText "If the field value is \"*\", the condition is true if the origin server has a current representation for the target resource."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3962]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "2. "
                  - StaticText "If the field value is a list of entity tags, the condition is true if any of the listed tags match the entity tag of the selected representation."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3963]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "3. "
                  - StaticText "Otherwise, the condition is false."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e3964]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "An origin server that evaluates an If-Match condition MUST NOT perform the requested method if the condition evaluates to false. Instead, the origin server MAY indicate that the conditional request failed by responding with a "
                - link "412 (Precondition Failed)" [ref=e3010]
                - StaticText " status code. Alternatively, if the request is a state-changing operation that appears to have already been applied to the selected representation, the origin server MAY respond with a "
                - link "2xx (Successful)" [ref=e3011]
                - StaticText " status code (i.e., the change requested by the user agent has already succeeded, but the user agent might not be aware of it, perhaps because the prior response was lost or an equivalent change was made by some other user agent)."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3012]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Allowing an origin server to send a success response when a change request appears to have already been applied is more efficient for many authoring use cases, but comes with some risk if multiple user agents are making change requests that are very similar but not cooperative. For example, multiple user agents writing to a common resource as a semaphore (e.g., a nonatomic increment) are likely to collide and potentially lose important state transitions. For those kinds of resources, an origin server is better off being stringent in sending 412 for every failed precondition on an unsafe method. In other cases, excluding the ETag field from a success response might encourage the user agent to perform a GET as its next request to eliminate confusion about the resource's current state."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3013]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A client MAY send an If-Match header field in a "
                - link "GET" [ref=e3014]
                - StaticText " request to indicate that it would prefer a "
                - link "412 (Precondition Failed)" [ref=e3015]
                - StaticText " response if the selected representation does not match. However, this is only useful in range requests ("
                - link "Section 14" [ref=e3016]
                - StaticText ") for completing a previously received partial representation when there is no desire for a new representation. "
                - link "If-Range" [ref=e3017]
                - StaticText " ("
                - link "Section 13.1.5" [ref=e3018]
                - StaticText ") is better suited for range requests when the client prefers to receive a new representation."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3019]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A cache or intermediary MAY ignore If-Match because its interoperability features are only necessary for an origin server."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3020]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Note that an If-Match header field with a list value containing \"*\" and other values (including other instances of \"*\") is syntactically invalid (therefore not allowed to be generated) and furthermore is unlikely to be interoperable."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3021]

                - StaticText "If-Modified-Since is typically used for two distinct purposes: 1) to allow efficient updates of a cached representation that does not have an entity tag and 2) to limit the scope of a web traversal to resources that have recently changed."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3059]

                - StaticText "When used for cache updates, a cache will typically use the value of the cached message's "

                - link "Date" [ref=e3061]

                - link "¶" [ref=e3063]

                - StaticText " header field received from the server in a prior response. Origin servers that choose an exact timestamp match based on the selected representation's "
                - link "Last-Modified" [ref=e3065]
                - StaticText " header field will not be able to help the user agent limit its data transfers to only those changed during the specified window."

              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Except when excluded below, a recipient cache or origin server MUST evaluate received request preconditions after it has successfully performed its normal request checks and just before it would process the request content (if any) or perform the action associated with the request method.                 - link "2xx (Successful)" [ref=e3145]
                - StaticText " or "
                - link "412 (Precondition Failed)" [ref=e3146]
                - StaticText ". In other words, redirects and failures that can be detected before significant processing occurs take precedence over the evaluation of preconditions."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3147]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A server that is not the origin server for the target resource and cannot act as a cache for requests on the target resource MUST NOT evaluate the conditional request header fields defined by this specification, and it MUST forward them if the request is forwarded, since the generating client intends that they be evaluated by a server that can provide a current representation. Likewise, a server MUST ignore the conditional request header fields defined by this specification when received with a request method that does not involve the selection or modification of a "
                - link "selected representation" [ref=e3148]
                - StaticText ", such as CONNECT, OPTIONS, or TRACE."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3149]

                - link "RFC8246" [expanded=false, ref=e3150]
                - StaticText "]) instructs caches to forgo forwarding conditional requests when they hold a fresh response."

          - heading "14. Range Requests" [level=2, ref=e40]
            - link "14. " [ref=e129]
            - link "Range Requests" [ref=e130]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Clients often encounter interrupted data transfers as a result of canceled requests or dropped connections. When a client has stored a partial representation, it is desirable to request the remainder of that representation in a subsequent request rather than transfer the entire representation. Likewise, devices with limited local storage might benefit from being able to request only a subset of a larger representation, such as a single page of a very large document, or the dimensions of an embedded image."
            - link "¶" [ref=e131]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Range requests are an OPTIONAL feature of HTTP, designed so that recipients not implementing this feature (or not supporting it for the target resource) can respond as if it is a normal GET request without impacting interoperability. Partial responses are indicated by a distinct status code to not be mistaken for full responses by caches that might not implement the feature."
            - link "¶" [ref=e132]

            - heading "14.1. Range Units" [level=3, ref=e303]
              - link "14.1. " [ref=e1164]
              - link "Range Units" [ref=e1165]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Representation data can be partitioned into subranges when there are addressable structural units inherent to that data's content coding or media type.             - heading "14.2. Range" [level=3, ref=e304]
              - link "14.2. " [ref=e1179]
              - link "Range" [ref=e1180]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The \"Range\" header field on a GET request modifies the method semantics to request transfer of only one or more subranges of the selected representation data ("
              - link "Section 8.1" [ref=e1181]
              - StaticText "), rather than the entire "
              - link "selected representation" [ref=e1182]
              - StaticText "."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1183]
            - generic
              - generic
                - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e1871]
                - status
                - StaticText "  Range = ranges-specifier\n"
              - link "¶" [ref=e1184]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server MAY ignore the Range header field. However, origin servers and intermediate caches ought to support byte ranges when possible, since they support efficient recovery from partially failed transfers and partial retrieval of large representations."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1185]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server MUST ignore a Range header field received with a request method that is unrecognized or for which range handling is not defined. For this specification, "
              - link "GET" [ref=e1186]
              - StaticText " is the only method for which range handling is defined."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1187]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "An origin server MUST ignore a Range header field that contains a range unit it does not understand. A proxy MAY discard a Range header field that contains a range unit it does not understand."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1188]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server that supports range requests MAY ignore or reject a "
              - link "Range" [ref=e1189]
              - StaticText " header field that contains an invalid "
              - link "ranges-specifier" [ref=e1190]
                - StaticText "ranges-specifier"
              - StaticText " ("
              - link "Section 14.1.1" [ref=e1191]
              - StaticText "), a "
              - link "ranges-specifier" [ref=e1192]
                - StaticText "ranges-specifier"
              - StaticText " with more than two overlapping ranges, or a set of many small ranges that are not listed in ascending order, since these are indications of either a broken client or a deliberate denial-of-service attack ("
              - link "Section 17.15" [ref=e1193]
              - StaticText "). A client SHOULD NOT request multiple ranges that are inherently less efficient to process and transfer than a single range that encompasses the same data."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1194]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A server that supports range requests MAY ignore a "
              - link "Range" [ref=e1195]
              - StaticText " header field when the selected representation has no content (i.e., the selected representation's data is of zero length)."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1196]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A client that is requesting multiple ranges SHOULD list those ranges in ascending order (the order in which they would typically be received in a complete representation) unless there is a specific need to request a later part earlier. For example, a user agent processing a large representation with an internal catalog of parts might need to request later parts first, particularly if the representation consists of pages stored in reverse order and the user agent wishes to transfer one page at a time."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1197]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The Range header field is evaluated after evaluating the precondition header fields defined in "
              - link "Section 13.1" [ref=e1198]
              - StaticText ", and only if the result in absence of the Range header field would be a "
              - link "200 (OK)" [ref=e1199]
              - StaticText " response. In other words, Range is ignored when a conditional GET would result in a "
              - link "304 (Not Modified)" [ref=e1200]
              - StaticText " response."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1201]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The If-Range header field ("
              - link "Section 13.1.5" [ref=e1202]
              - StaticText ") can be used as a precondition to applying the Range header field."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1203]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "If all of the preconditions are true, the server supports the Range header field for the target resource, the received Range field-value contains a valid "
              - link "ranges-specifier" [ref=e1204]
                - StaticText "ranges-specifier"
              - StaticText " with a "
              - link "range-unit" [ref=e1205]
              - StaticText " supported for that target resource, and that "
              - link "ranges-specifier" [ref=e1206]
                - StaticText "ranges-specifier"
              - StaticText " is "
              - link "satisfiable" [ref=e1207]
              - StaticText " with respect to the selected representation, the server SHOULD send a "
              - link "206 (Partial Content)" [ref=e1208]
              - StaticText " response with content containing one or more partial representations that correspond to the satisfiable "
              - link "range-spec" [ref=e1209]
              - StaticText "(s) requested."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1210]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The above does not imply that a server will send all requested ranges. In some cases, it may only be possible (or efficient) to send a portion of the requested ranges first, while expecting the client to re-request the remaining portions later if they are still desired (see "
              - link "Section 15.3.7" [ref=e1211]
              - StaticText ")."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1212]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "If all of the preconditions are true, the server supports the Range header field for the target resource, the received Range field-value contains a valid "
              - link "ranges-specifier" [ref=e1213]
                - StaticText "ranges-specifier"
              - StaticText ", and either the "
              - link "range-unit" [ref=e1214]
              - StaticText " is not supported for that target resource or the "
              - link "ranges-specifier" [ref=e1215]
                - StaticText "ranges-specifier"
              - StaticText " is unsatisfiable with respect to the selected representation, the server SHOULD send a "
              - link "416 (Range Not Satisfiable)" [ref=e1216]
              - StaticText " response."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1217]

              - link "¶" [ref=e1229]

              - link "¶" [ref=e1232]

              - link "¶" [ref=e1233]

              - link "¶" [ref=e1249]

          - heading "15. Status Codes" [level=2, ref=e41]
            - link "15. " [ref=e133]
            - link "Status Codes" [ref=e134]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "The status code of a response is a three-digit integer code that describes the result of the request and the semantics of the response, including whether the request was successful and what content is enclosed (if any). All valid status codes are within the range of 100 to 599, inclusive."
            - link "¶" [ref=e135]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "The first digit of the status code defines the class of response. The last two digits do not have any categorization role. There are five values for the first digit:"
            - link "¶" [ref=e136]
          - list
            - listitem [level=1]
              - ListMarker "• "
              - link "1xx (Informational)" [ref=e309]
              - StaticText ": The request was received, continuing process"
              - link "¶" [ref=e310]
            - listitem [level=1]
              - ListMarker "• "
              - link "2xx (Successful)" [ref=e311]
              - StaticText ": The request was successfully received, understood, and accepted"
              - link "¶" [ref=e312]
            - listitem [level=1]
              - ListMarker "• "
              - link "3xx (Redirection)" [ref=e313]
              - StaticText ": Further action needs to be taken in order to complete the request"
              - link "¶" [ref=e314]
            - listitem [level=1]
              - ListMarker "• "
              - link "4xx (Client Error)" [ref=e315]
              - StaticText ": The request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled"
              - link "¶" [ref=e316]
            - listitem [level=1]
              - ListMarker "• "
              - link "5xx (Server Error)" [ref=e317]
              - StaticText ": The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request"
              - link "¶" [ref=e318]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "HTTP status codes are extensible. A client is not required to understand the meaning of all registered status codes, though such understanding is obviously desirable. However, a client MUST understand the class of any status code, as indicated by the first digit, and treat an unrecognized status code as being equivalent to the x00 status code of that class."
            - link "¶" [ref=e137]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "For example, if a client receives an unrecognized status code of 471, it can see from the first digit that there was something wrong with its request and treat the response as if it had received a "
            - link "400 (Bad Request)" [ref=e138]
            - StaticText " status code. The response message will usually contain a representation that explains the status."
            - link "¶" [ref=e139]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Values outside the range 100..599 are invalid. Implementations often use three-digit integer values outside of that range (i.e., 600..999) for internal communication of non-HTTP status (e.g., library errors). A client that receives a response with an invalid status code SHOULD process the response as if it had a "
            - link "5xx (Server Error)" [ref=e140]
            - StaticText " status code."
            - link "¶" [ref=e141]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "A single request can have multiple associated responses: zero or more \"interim\" (non-final) responses with status codes in the \"informational\" ("
            - link "1xx" [ref=e319]
            - StaticText ") range, followed by exactly one \"final\" response with a status code in one of the other ranges."
            - link "¶" [ref=e320]
          - generic
            - heading "15.1. Overview of Status Codes" [level=3, ref=e321]
              - link "15.1. " [ref=e1296]
              - link "Overview of Status Codes" [ref=e1297]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The status codes listed below are defined in this specification. The reason phrases listed here are only recommendations -- they can be replaced by local equivalents or left out altogether without affecting the protocol."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1298]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "Responses with status codes that are defined as heuristically cacheable (e.g., 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, and 501 in this specification) can be reused by a cache with heuristic expiration unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls ["
              - link "CACHING" [ref=e1299]
              - StaticText "]; all other status codes are not heuristically cacheable."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1300]

              - StaticText "Additional status codes, outside the scope of this specification, have been specified for use in HTTP. All such status codes ought to be registered within the \"Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Status Code Registry\", as described in "
              - link "Section 16.2" [ref=e1301]

              - link "Informational 1xx" [ref=e1304]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "The 1xx (Informational) class of status code indicates an interim response for communicating connection status or request progress prior to completing the requested action and sending a final response. Since HTTP/1.0 did not define any 1xx status codes, a server MUST NOT send a 1xx response to an HTTP/1.0 client."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1305]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A 1xx response is terminated by the end of the header section; it cannot contain content or trailers."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1306]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A client MUST be able to parse one or more 1xx responses received prior to a final response, even if the client does not expect one. A user agent MAY ignore unexpected 1xx responses."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1307]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "A proxy MUST forward 1xx responses unless the proxy itself requested the generation of the 1xx response. For example, if a proxy adds an \"Expect: 100-continue\" header field when it forwards a request, then it need not forward the corresponding "
              - link "100 (Continue)" [ref=e1308]

              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The 202 (Accepted) status code indicates that the request has been accepted for processing, but the processing has not been completed. The request might or might not eventually be acted upon, as it might be disallowed when processing actually takes place. There is no facility in HTTP for re-sending a status code from an asynchronous operation."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3261]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The 202 response is intentionally noncommittal. Its purpose is to allow a server to accept a request for some other process (perhaps a batch-oriented process that is only run once per day) without requiring that the user agent's connection to the server persist until the process is completed. The representation sent with this response ought to describe the request's current status and point to (or embed) a status monitor that can provide the user with an estimate of when the request will be fulfilled."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3262]

              - heading "15.3.5. 204 No Content" [level=4, ref=e1907]
                - link "15.3.5. " [ref=e3271]
                - link "204 No Content" [ref=e3272]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The 204 (No Content) status code indicates that the server has successfully fulfilled the request and that there is no additional content to send in the response content. Metadata in the response header fields refer to the "
                - link "target resource" [ref=e3273]
                - StaticText " and its "
                - link "selected representation" [ref=e3274]
                - StaticText " after the requested action was applied."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3275]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For example, if a 204 status code is received in response to a PUT request and the response contains an "
                - link "ETag" [ref=e3276]
                - StaticText " field, then the PUT was successful and the ETag field value contains the entity tag for the new representation of that target resource."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3277]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The 204 response allows a server to indicate that the action has been successfully applied to the target resource, while implying that the user agent does not need to traverse away from its current \"document view\" (if any). The server assumes that the user agent will provide some indication of the success to its user, in accord with its own interface, and apply any new or updated metadata in the response to its active representation."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3278]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For example, a 204 status code is commonly used with document editing interfaces corresponding to a \"save\" action, such that the document being saved remains available to the user for editing. It is also frequently used with interfaces that expect automated data transfers to be prevalent, such as within distributed version control systems."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3279]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A 204 response is terminated by the end of the header section; it cannot contain content or trailers."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3280]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A 204 response is heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls (see "
                - link "Section 4.2.2" [expanded=false, ref=e3281]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "CACHING" [ref=e3282]
                - StaticText "])."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3283]
            - generic
              - heading "15.3.6. 205 Reset Content" [level=4, ref=e1908]
                - link "15.3.6. " [ref=e3284]
                - link "205 Reset Content" [ref=e3285]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The 205 (Reset Content) status code indicates that the server has fulfilled the request and desires that the user agent reset the \"document view\", which caused the request to be sent, to its original state as received from the origin server."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3286]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "This response is intended to support a common data entry use case where the user receives content that supports data entry (a form, notepad, canvas, etc.), enters or manipulates data in that space, causes the entered data to be submitted in a request, and then the data entry mechanism is reset for the next entry so that the user can easily initiate another input action."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3287]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Since the 205 status code implies that no additional content will be provided, a server MUST NOT generate content in a 205 response."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3288]

                - StaticText "The 206 (Partial Content) status code indicates that the server is successfully fulfilling a range request for the target resource by transferring one or more parts of the "

                - StaticText "."

              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A server that supports range requests ("
                - link "Section 14" [ref=e3293]
                - StaticText ") will usually attempt to satisfy all of the requested ranges, since sending less data will likely result in another client request for the remainder.                   - link "¶" [ref=e4814]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "When multiple ranges are requested, a server MAY coalesce any of the ranges that overlap, or that are separated by a gap that is smaller than the overhead of sending multiple parts, regardless of the order in which the corresponding range-spec appeared in the received "
                  - link "Range" [ref=e4815]
                  - StaticText " header field. Since the typical overhead between each part of a \"multipart/byteranges\" is around 80 bytes, depending on the selected representation's media type and the chosen boundary parameter length, it can be less efficient to transfer many small disjoint parts than it is to transfer the entire selected representation."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4816]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "A server MUST NOT generate a multipart response to a request for a single range, since a client that does not request multiple parts might not support multipart responses. However, a server MAY generate a \"multipart/byteranges\" response with only a single body part if multiple ranges were requested and only one range was found to be satisfiable or only one range remained after coalescing. A client that cannot process a \"multipart/byteranges\" response MUST NOT generate a request that asks for multiple ranges."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4817]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "A server that generates a multipart response SHOULD send the parts in the same order that the corresponding range-spec appeared in the received "
                  - link "Range" [ref=e4818]
                  - StaticText " header field, excluding those ranges that were deemed unsatisfiable or that were coalesced into other ranges. A client that receives a multipart response MUST inspect the "
                  - link "Content-Range" [ref=e4819]
                  - StaticText " header field present in each body part in order to determine which range is contained in that body part; a client cannot rely on receiving the same ranges that it requested, nor the same order that it requested."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4820]

                - heading "15.3.7.3. Combining Parts" [level=5, ref=e4023]
                  - link "15.3.7.3. " [ref=e4821]
                  - link "Combining Parts" [ref=e4822]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "A response might transfer only a subrange of a representation if the connection closed prematurely or if the request used one or more Range specifications. After several such transfers, a client might have received several ranges of the same representation. These ranges can only be safely combined if they all have in common the same strong validator ("
                  - link "Section 8.8.1" [ref=e4823]
                  - StaticText ")."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4824]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "A client that has received multiple partial responses to GET requests on a target resource MAY combine those responses into a larger continuous range if they share the same strong validator."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4825]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "If the most recent response is an incomplete "
                  - link "200 (OK)" [ref=e4826]
                  - StaticText " response, then the header fields of that response are used for any combined response and replace those of the matching stored responses."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4827]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "If the most recent response is a "
                  - link "206 (Partial Content)" [ref=e4828]
                  - StaticText " response and at least one of the matching stored responses is a "
                  - link "200 (OK)" [ref=e4829]
                  - StaticText ", then the combined response header fields consist of the most recent 200 response's header fields. If all of the matching stored responses are 206 responses, then the stored response with the most recent header fields is used as the source of header fields for the combined response, except that the client MUST use other header fields provided in the new response, aside from "
                  - link "Content-Range" [ref=e4830]
                  - StaticText ", to replace all instances of the corresponding header fields in the stored response."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4831]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "The combined response content consists of the union of partial content ranges within the new response and all of the matching stored responses. If the union consists of the entire range of the representation, then the client MUST process the combined response as if it were a complete "
                  - link "200 (OK)" [ref=e4832]
                  - StaticText " response, including a "
                  - link "Content-Length" [ref=e4833]
                  - StaticText " header field that reflects the complete length. Otherwise, the client MUST process the set of continuous ranges as one of the following: an incomplete "
                  - link "200 (OK)" [ref=e4834]
                  - StaticText " response if the combined response is a prefix of the representation, a single "
                  - link "206 (Partial Content)" [ref=e4835]
                  - StaticText " response containing \"multipart/byteranges\" content, or multiple "
                  - link "206 (Partial Content)" [ref=e4836]
                  - StaticText " responses, each with one continuous range that is indicated by a "
                  - link "Content-Range" [ref=e4837]
                  - StaticText " header field."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4838]

              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The 300 (Multiple Choices) status code indicates that the "
                - link "target resource" [ref=e3328]
                - StaticText " has more than one representation, each with its own more specific identifier, and information about the alternatives is being provided so that the user (or user agent) can select a preferred representation by redirecting its request to one or more of those identifiers. In other words, the server desires that the user agent engage in reactive negotiation to select the most appropriate representation(s) for its needs ("
                - link "Section 12" [ref=e3329]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3330]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "If the server has a preferred choice, the server SHOULD generate a "
                - link "Location" [ref=e3331]
                - StaticText " header field containing a preferred choice's URI reference. The user agent MAY use the Location field value for automatic redirection."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3332]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For request methods other than HEAD, the server SHOULD generate content in the 300 response containing a list of representation metadata and URI reference(s) from which the user or user agent can choose the one most preferred. The user agent MAY make a selection from that list automatically if it understands the provided media type. A specific format for automatic selection is not defined by this specification because HTTP tries to remain orthogonal to the definition of its content. In practice, the representation is provided in some easily parsed format believed to be acceptable to the user agent, as determined by shared design or content negotiation, or in some commonly accepted hypertext format."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3333]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A 300 response is heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls (see "
                - link "Section 4.2.2" [expanded=false, ref=e3334]
                - StaticText " of ["
                - link "CACHING" [ref=e3335]
                - StaticText "])."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3336]
              - paragraph
                - strong
                  - StaticText "Note:"
                - StaticText " The original proposal for the 300 status code defined the URI header field as providing a list of alternative representations, such that it would be usable for 200, 300, and 406 responses and be transferred in responses to the HEAD method. However, lack of deployment and disagreement over syntax led to both URI and Alternates (a subsequent proposal) being dropped from this specification. It is possible to communicate the list as a Link header field value ["
                - link "RFC8288" [expanded=false, ref=e4036]
                - StaticText "] whose members have a relationship of \"alternate\", though deployment is a chicken-and-egg problem."

                - link "target resource" [ref=e3339]

              - heading "15.4.4. 303 See Other" [level=4, ref=e1940]
                - link "15.4.4. " [ref=e3351]
                - link "303 See Other" [ref=e3352]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The 303 (See Other) status code indicates that the server is redirecting the user agent to a different resource, as indicated by a URI in the "
                - link "Location" [ref=e3353]
                - StaticText " header field, which is intended to provide an indirect response to the original request. A user agent can perform a retrieval request targeting that URI (a GET or HEAD request if using HTTP), which might also be redirected, and present the eventual result as an answer to the original request. Note that the new URI in the Location header field is not considered equivalent to the target URI."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3354]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "This status code is applicable to any HTTP method. It is primarily used to allow the output of a POST action to redirect the user agent to a different resource, since doing so provides the information corresponding to the POST response as a resource that can be separately identified, bookmarked, and cached."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3355]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A 303 response to a GET request indicates that the origin server does not have a representation of the "
                - link "target resource" [ref=e3356]
                - StaticText " that can be transferred by the server over HTTP. However, the "
                - link "Location" [ref=e3357]
                - StaticText " field value refers to a resource that is descriptive of the target resource, such that making a retrieval request on that other resource might result in a representation that is useful to recipients without implying that it represents the original target resource. Note that answers to the questions of what can be represented, what representations are adequate, and what might be a useful description are outside the scope of HTTP."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3358]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Except for responses to a HEAD request, the representation of a 303 response ought to contain a short hypertext note with a hyperlink to the same URI reference provided in the "
                - link "Location" [ref=e3359]
                - StaticText " header field."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3360]

                - StaticText " defines what makes a bytes range set satisfiable."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3507]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A server that generates a 416 response to a byte-range request SHOULD generate a "
                - link "Content-Range" [ref=e3508]
                - StaticText " header field specifying the current length of the selected representation ("
                - link "Section 14.4" [ref=e3509]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3510]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "For example:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3511]

                - generic
                  - button "Copy to clipboard" [ref=e4052]

                  - StaticText "HTTP/1.1 416 Range Not Satisfiable\nDate: Fri, 20 Jan 2012 15:41:54 GMT\nContent-Range: bytes */47022\n"

              - paragraph
                - strong
                  - StaticText "Note:"
                - StaticText " Because servers are free to ignore "
                - link "Range" [ref=e4053]
                - StaticText ", many implementations will respond with the entire selected representation in a "
                - link "200 (OK)" [ref=e4054]
                - StaticText " response. That is partly because most clients are prepared to receive a "
                - link "200 (OK)" [ref=e4055]
                - StaticText " to complete the task (albeit less efficiently) and partly because clients might not stop making an invalid range request until they have received a complete representation. Thus, clients cannot depend on receiving a "
                - link "416 (Range Not Satisfiable)" [ref=e4056]
                - StaticText " response even when it is most appropriate."

            - link "16. " [ref=e142]
            - link "Extending HTTP" [ref=e143]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "HTTP defines a number of generic extension points that can be used to introduce capabilities to the protocol without introducing a new version, including methods, status codes, field names, and further extensibility points within defined fields, such as authentication schemes and cache directives (see Cache-Control extensions in "
            - link "Section 5.2.3" [expanded=false, ref=e144]
            - StaticText " of ["
            - link "CACHING" [ref=e145]
            - StaticText "]). Because the semantics of HTTP are not versioned, these extension points are persistent; the version of the protocol in use does not affect their semantics."
            - link "¶" [ref=e146]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Version-independent extensions are discouraged from depending on or interacting with the specific version of the protocol in use. When this is unavoidable, careful consideration needs to be given to how the extension can interoperate across versions."
            - link "¶" [ref=e147]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Additionally, specific versions of HTTP might have their own extensibility points, such as transfer codings in HTTP/1.1 ("
            - link "Section 6.1" [expanded=false, ref=e148]

            - link "HTTP/1.1" [ref=e149]
            - StaticText "]) and HTTP/2 SETTINGS or frame types (["
            - link "HTTP/2" [ref=e150]
            - StaticText "]). These extension points are specific to the version of the protocol they occur within."
            - link "¶" [ref=e151]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "Version-specific extensions cannot override or modify the semantics of a version-independent mechanism or extension point (like a method or header field) without explicitly being allowed by that protocol element. For example, the CONNECT method ("
            - link "Section 9.3.6" [ref=e152]
            - StaticText ") allows this."
            - link "¶" [ref=e153]
          - paragraph
            - StaticText "These guidelines assure that the protocol operates correctly and predictably, even when parts of the path implement different versions of HTTP."

              - heading "16.1.2. Considerations for New Methods" [level=4, ref=e1975]
                - link "16.1.2. " [ref=e3576]
                - link "Considerations for New Methods" [ref=e3577]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Standardized methods are generic; that is, they are potentially applicable to any resource, not just one particular media type, kind of resource, or application. As such, it is preferred that new methods be registered in a document that isn't specific to a single application or data format, since orthogonal technologies deserve orthogonal specification."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3578]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Since message parsing ("
                - link "Section 6" [ref=e3579]
                - StaticText ") needs to be independent of method semantics (aside from responses to HEAD), definitions of new methods cannot change the parsing algorithm or prohibit the presence of content on either the request or the response message. Definitions of new methods can specify that only a zero-length content is allowed by requiring a Content-Length header field with a value of \"0\"."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3580]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Likewise, new methods cannot use the special host:port and asterisk forms of request target that are allowed for "
                - link "CONNECT" [ref=e3581]
                - StaticText " and "
                - link "OPTIONS" [ref=e3582]
                - StaticText ", respectively ("
                - link "Section 7.1" [ref=e3583]
                - StaticText "). A full URI in absolute form is needed for the target URI, which means either the request target needs to be sent in absolute form or the target URI will be reconstructed from the request context in the same way it is for other methods."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3584]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "A new method definition needs to indicate whether it is safe ("
                - link "Section 9.2.1" [ref=e3585]
                - StaticText "), idempotent ("
                - link "Section 9.2.2" [ref=e3586]
                - StaticText "), cacheable ("
                - link "Section 9.2.3" [ref=e3587]
                - StaticText "), what semantics are to be associated with the request content (if any), and what refinements the method makes to header field or status code semantics. If the new method is cacheable, its definition ought to describe how, and under what conditions, a cache can store a response and use it to satisfy a subsequent request. The new method ought to describe whether it can be made conditional ("
                - link "Section 13.1" [ref=e3588]
                - StaticText ") and, if so, how a server responds when the condition is false. Likewise, if the new method might have some use for partial response semantics ("
                - link "Section 14.2" [ref=e3589]
                - StaticText "), it ought to document this, too."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3590]
              - paragraph
                - strong
                  - StaticText "Note:"
                - StaticText " Avoid defining a method name that starts with \"M-\", since that prefix might be misinterpreted as having the semantics assigned to it by ["
                - link "RFC2774" [expanded=false, ref=e4067]
                - StaticText "]."
                - link "¶" [ref=e4068]

            - generic
              - heading "16.2.2. Considerations for New Status Codes" [level=4, ref=e1977]
                - link "16.2.2. " [ref=e3599]
                - link "Considerations for New Status Codes" [ref=e3600]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "When it is necessary to express semantics for a response that are not defined by current status codes, a new status code can be registered. Status codes are generic; they are potentially applicable to any resource, not just one particular media type, kind of resource, or application of HTTP. As such, it is preferred that new status codes be registered in a document that isn't specific to a single application."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3601]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "New status codes are required to fall under one of the categories defined in "
                - link "Section 15" [ref=e3602]
                - StaticText ". To allow existing parsers to process the response message, new status codes cannot disallow content, although they can mandate a zero-length content."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3603]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Proposals for new status codes that are not yet widely deployed ought to avoid allocating a specific number for the code until there is clear consensus that it will be registered; instead, early drafts can use a notation such as \"4NN\", or \"3N0\" .. \"3N9\", to indicate the class of the proposed status code(s) without consuming a number prematurely."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3604]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The definition of a new status code ought to explain the request conditions that would cause a response containing that status code (e.g., combinations of request header fields and/or method(s)) along with any dependencies on response header fields (e.g., what fields are required, what fields can modify the semantics, and what field semantics are further refined when used with the new status code)."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3605]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "By default, a status code applies only to the request corresponding to the response it occurs within. If a status code applies to a larger scope of applicability -- for example, all requests to the resource in question or all requests to a server -- this must be explicitly specified. When doing so, it should be noted that not all clients can be expected to consistently apply a larger scope because they might not understand the new status code."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3606]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The definition of a new final status code ought to specify whether or not it is heuristically cacheable. Note that any response with a final status code can be cached if the response has explicit freshness information. A status code defined as heuristically cacheable is allowed to be cached without explicit freshness information. Likewise, the definition of a status code can place constraints upon cache behavior if the must-understand cache directive is used. See ["
                - link "CACHING" [ref=e3607]
                - StaticText "] for more information."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3608]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Finally, the definition of a new status code ought to indicate whether the content has any implied association with an identified resource ("
                - link "Section 6.4.2" [ref=e3609]
                - StaticText ")."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3610]
          - generic
            - heading "16.3. Field Extensibility" [level=3, ref=e329]
              - link "16.3. " [ref=e1333]
              - link "Field Extensibility" [ref=e1334]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "HTTP's most widely used extensibility point is the definition of new header and trailer fields."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1335]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "New fields can be defined such that, when they are understood by a recipient, they override or enhance the interpretation of previously defined fields, define preconditions on request evaluation, or refine the meaning of responses."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1336]
            - paragraph
              - StaticText "However, defining a field doesn't guarantee its deployment or recognition by recipients. Most fields are designed with the expectation that a recipient can safely ignore (but forward downstream) any field not recognized. In other cases, the sender's ability to understand a given field might be indicated by its prior communication, perhaps in the protocol version or fields that it sent in prior messages, or its use of a specific media type. Likewise, direct inspection of support might be possible through an OPTIONS request or by interacting with a defined well-known URI ["
              - link "RFC8615" [expanded=false, ref=e1337]
              - StaticText "] if such inspection is defined along with the field being introduced."
              - link "¶" [ref=e1338]

                - definition
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "The expert(s) can define additional fields to be collected in the registry, in consultation with the community."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3623]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Standards-defined names have a status of \"permanent\". Other names can also be registered as permanent if the expert(s) finds that they are in use, in consultation with the community. Other names should be registered as \"provisional\"."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3624]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Provisional entries can be removed by the expert(s) if -- in consultation with the community -- the expert(s) find that they are not in use. The expert(s) can change a provisional entry's status to permanent at any time."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3625]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Note that names can be registered by third parties (including the expert(s)) if the expert(s) determines that an unregistered name is widely deployed and not likely to be registered in a timely manner otherwise."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3626]
            - generic
              - heading "16.3.2. Considerations for New Fields" [level=4, ref=e1979]
                - link "16.3.2. " [ref=e3627]
                - link "Considerations for New Fields" [ref=e3628]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "HTTP header and trailer fields are a widely used extension point for the protocol. While they can be used in an ad hoc fashion, fields that are intended for wider use need to be carefully documented to ensure interoperability."
                - link "¶" [ref=e3629]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "In particular, authors of specifications defining new fields are advised to consider and, where appropriate, document the following aspects:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3630]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "Under what conditions the field can be used; e.g., only in responses or requests, in all messages, only on responses to a particular request method, etc."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4077]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "Whether the field semantics are further refined by their context, such as their use with certain request methods or status codes."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4078]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "The scope of applicability for the information conveyed. By default, fields apply only to the message they are associated with, but some response fields are designed to apply to all representations of a resource, the resource itself, or an even broader scope. Specifications that expand the scope of a response field will need to carefully consider issues such as content negotiation, the time period of applicability, and (in some cases) multi-tenant server deployments."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4079]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "Under what conditions intermediaries are allowed to insert, delete, or modify the field's value."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4080]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "If the field is allowable in trailers; by default, it will not be (see "
                  - link "Section 6.5.1" [ref=e4081]
                  - StaticText ")."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4082]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "Whether it is appropriate or even required to list the field name in the "
                  - link "Connection" [ref=e4083]
                  - StaticText " header field (i.e., if the field is to be hop-by-hop; see "
                  - link "Section 7.6.1" [ref=e4084]
                  - StaticText ")."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4085]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "Whether the field introduces any additional security considerations, such as disclosure of privacy-related data."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4086]
              - paragraph
                - StaticText "Request header fields have additional considerations that need to be documented if the default behavior is not appropriate:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3631]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - StaticText "If it is appropriate to list the field name in a "

                  - link "Section 12.5.5" [ref=e4088]

              - generic
                - heading "16.3.2.1. Considerations for New Field Names" [level=5, ref=e4094]
                  - link "16.3.2.1. " [ref=e4839]
                  - link "Considerations for New Field Names" [ref=e4840]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Authors of specifications defining new fields are advised to choose a short but descriptive field name. Short names avoid needless data transmission; descriptive names avoid confusion and \"squatting\" on names that might have broader uses."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4841]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "To that end, limited-use fields (such as a header confined to a single application or use case) are encouraged to use a name that includes that use (or an abbreviation) as a prefix; for example, if the Foo Application needs a Description field, it might use \"Foo-Desc\"; \"Description\" is too generic, and \"Foo-Description\" is needlessly long."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4842]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "While the field-name syntax is defined to allow any token character, in practice some implementations place limits on the characters they accept in field-names. To be interoperable, new field names SHOULD constrain themselves to alphanumeric characters, \"-\", and \".\", and SHOULD begin with a letter. For example, the underscore (\"_\") character can be problematic when passed through non-HTTP gateway interfaces (see "
                  - link "Section 17.10" [ref=e4843]
                  - StaticText ")."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4844]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Field names ought not be prefixed with \"X-\"; see ["
                  - link "BCP178" [ref=e4845]
                  - StaticText "] for further information."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4846]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Other prefixes are sometimes used in HTTP field names; for example, \"Accept-\" is used in many content negotiation headers, and \"Content-\" is used as explained in "
                  - link "Section 6.4" [ref=e4847]
                  - StaticText ". These prefixes are only an aid to recognizing the purpose of a field and do not trigger automatic processing."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4848]
              - generic
                - heading "16.3.2.2. Considerations for New Field Values" [level=5, ref=e4095]
                  - link "16.3.2.2. " [ref=e4849]
                  - link "Considerations for New Field Values" [ref=e4850]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "A major task in the definition of a new HTTP field is the specification of the field value syntax: what senders should generate, and how recipients should infer semantics from what is received."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4851]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Authors are encouraged (but not required) to use either the ABNF rules in this specification or those in ["
                  - link "RFC8941" [expanded=false, ref=e4852]
                  - StaticText "] to define the syntax of new field values."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4853]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Authors are advised to carefully consider how the combination of multiple field lines will impact them (see "
                  - link "Section 5.3" [ref=e4854]
                  - StaticText "). Because senders might erroneously send multiple values, and both intermediaries and HTTP libraries can perform combination automatically, this applies to all field values -- even when only a single value is anticipated."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4855]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Therefore, authors are advised to delimit or encode values that contain commas (e.g., with the "
                  - link "quoted-string" [ref=e4856]
                  - StaticText " rule of "
                  - link "Section 5.6.4" [ref=e4857]
                  - StaticText ", the String data type of ["
                  - link "RFC8941" [expanded=false, ref=e4858]
                  - StaticText "], or a field-specific encoding). This ensures that commas within field data are not confused with the commas that delimit a list value."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4859]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "For example, the "
                  - link "Content-Type" [ref=e4860]
                  - StaticText " field value only allows commas inside quoted strings, which can be reliably parsed even when multiple values are present. The "
                  - link "Location" [ref=e4861]
                  - StaticText " field value provides a counter-example that should not be emulated: because URIs can include commas, it is not possible to reliably distinguish between a single value that includes a comma from two values."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4862]
                - paragraph
                  - StaticText "Authors of fields with a singleton value (see "
                  - link "Section 5.5" [ref=e4863]
                  - StaticText ") are additionally advised to document how to treat messages where the multiple members are present (a sensible default would be to ignore the field, but this might not always be the right choice)."
                  - link "¶" [ref=e4864]

              - paragraph
                - StaticText "There are certain aspects of the HTTP Authentication framework that put constraints on how new authentication schemes can work:"
                - link "¶" [ref=e3642]
              - list
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - paragraph
                    - StaticText "HTTP authentication is presumed to be stateless: all of the information necessary to authenticate a request MUST be provided in the request, rather than be dependent on the server remembering prior requests. Authentication based on, or bound to, the underlying connection is outside the scope of this specification and inherently flawed unless steps are taken to ensure that the connection cannot be used by any party other than the authenticated user (see "
                    - link "Section 3.3" [ref=e4865]
                    - StaticText ")."
                    - link "¶" [ref=e4866]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - paragraph
                    - StaticText "The authentication parameter \"realm\" is reserved for defining protection spaces as described in "
                    - link "Section 11.5" [ref=e4867]
                    - StaticText ". New schemes MUST NOT use it in a way incompatible with that definition."
                    - link "¶" [ref=e4868]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - paragraph
                    - StaticText "The \"token68\" notation was introduced for compatibility with existing authentication schemes and can only be used once per challenge or credential.                     - link "¶" [ref=e4869]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - paragraph
                    - StaticText "The parsing of challenges and credentials is defined by this specification and cannot be modified by new authentication schemes. When the auth-param syntax is used, all parameters ought to support both token and quoted-string syntax, and syntactical constraints ought to be defined on the field value after parsing (i.e., quoted-string processing). This is necessary so that recipients can use a generic parser that applies to all authentication schemes."
                    - link "¶" [ref=e4870]
                  - paragraph
                    - strong
                      - StaticText "Note:"
                    - StaticText " The fact that the value syntax for the \"realm\" parameter is restricted to quoted-string was a bad design choice not to be repeated for new parameters."
                    - link "¶" [ref=e4871]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - paragraph
                    - StaticText "Definitions of new schemes ought to define the treatment of unknown extension parameters. In general, a \"must-ignore\" rule is preferable to a \"must-understand\" rule, because otherwise it will be hard to introduce new parameters in the presence of legacy recipients. Furthermore, it's good to describe the policy for defining new parameters (such as \"update the specification\" or \"use this registry\")."
                    - link "¶" [ref=e4872]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - paragraph
                    - StaticText "Authentication schemes need to document whether they are usable in origin-server authentication (i.e., using "

                    - link "Proxy-Authenticate" [ref=e4874]

                    - StaticText ")."
                    - link "¶" [ref=e4875]
                - listitem [level=1]
                  - ListMarker "• "
                  - paragraph
                    - StaticText "The credentials carried in an "
                    - link "Authorization" [ref=e4876]
                    - StaticText " header field are specific to the user agent and, therefore, have the same effect on HTTP caches as the \"private\" cache response directive ("
                    - link "Section 5.2.2.7" [expanded=false, ref=e4877]
                    - StaticText " of ["
                    - link "CACHING" [ref=e4878]
                    - StaticText "]), within the scope of the request in which they appear."
                    - link "¶" [ref=e4879]

                    - link "Authorization" [ref=e4880]
